facts.value: Pricing page says Free 1 member and unlimited on Start/Grow/Scale. A recent Free-plan blog says Start has up to 5 members. Current pricing page is used for the main plan value; Start seat allowance conflicts across official pages.

facts.label: Workflow count and processing operations
facts.value: Plans list 1 workflow on Free/Start, 3 on Grow, and 5 on Scale; Enterprise custom. Current public pricing lists task and execution counts as unlimited, while workflow executions still have a published per-execution charge.

facts.label: Inactivity, pause and deletion
facts.value: No idle-account sleep, pause, or inactivity-based file deletion interval was found in pricing, docs, FAQ, privacy, or linked Service Terms.

facts.label: Free quota exhaustion
facts.value: Free accounts may be blocked at quota and resume at the next billing-cycle reset or after upgrade; monthly uploads, bandwidth and transformations reset, while stored-file size remains until deletion.

facts.label: Lowest paid commitment
facts.value: Start is the lowest listed paid plan at $69 billed monthly. It is not a separate usage-only plan.

facts.label: Annual billing
facts.value: Grow is displayed at $90/month and $1,079.88 billed annually; Scale at $100/month and $1,199.88 billed annually. Both published annual totals are $0.12 below twelve times the displayed monthly amount; values are kept as shown, not silently reconciled.

facts.label: Enterprise price
facts.value: Enterprise price is custom; no public starting price or minimum commitment is stated.

facts.label: Currency and tax
facts.value: Service Terms say fees are payable in USD and listed fees exclude applicable sales/VAT-like taxes.

facts.label: Billing cycle and usage reset
facts.value: Plan prices and allotments are monthly; Service Terms define a monthly billing cycle from activation. Usage counters reset at the start of each cycle/month according to plan FAQ; exact timezone is not stated.

facts.label: Start overage rates
facts.value: Start monthly overages: bandwidth $0.20/GB; uploads $0.006 each; transformations $0.0025 each; Filestack storage $0.50/GB.

facts.label: Grow overage rates
facts.value: Grow monthly overages: bandwidth $0.15/GB; uploads $0.005 each; transformations $0.002 each; Filestack storage $0.375/GB.

facts.label: Scale overage rates
facts.value: Scale monthly overages: bandwidth $0.10/GB; uploads $0.004 each; transformations $0.00125 each; Filestack storage $0.25/GB.

facts.label: Enterprise overages
facts.value: Enterprise overage limits and rates are custom.

facts.label: Upload meter
facts.value: Each file uploaded counts as one upload; uploading several files counts each file separately. Re-uploading a file is described as a new upload.

facts.label: Upload overwrite detail
facts.value: A recent official Free-plan article says overwriting an existing handle is not a new upload, while the product FAQ says each upload operation/re-upload counts as one. Whether a specific overwrite path is exempt is unclear across these descriptions.

facts.label: Transformation meter
facts.value: A modified file counts against the transformation quota. A chained URL with several parameters counts as one transformation during the default 30-day cache period.

facts.label: Transformation cache and URL variants
facts.value: A repeated request for a cached transformation URL does not create a new general transformation during its cache period; changing URL parameter order can count as a new transformation. The default transformation cache is 30 days.

facts.label: Video and audio transformation meter
facts.value: Video/audio conversion uses output duration and quality: SD video 2 transformation units/second, HD 3, UHD 6; audio 3/second. Current price table additionally lists video conversion units (VCUs): SD 1/second, HD 2, UHD 6.

facts.label: Video conversion availability and overage
facts.value: Video conversions are listed on Grow and Scale with 3,000 units/month and $0.025 per unit overage; Enterprise custom.

facts.label: Workflow execution pricing
facts.value: Workflow executions are priced separately: Start $0.02 per execution, Grow $0.0175, Scale $0.015; Enterprise custom.

facts.label: Paid-plan AI/document task units
facts.value: Start/Grow/Scale list the same monthly task allowances and USD overages: OCR 5,000 then $0.03/unit; Envelope OCR 1,000 then $0.03; Document Detection 1,000 then $0.20; Image Enhancement 1,000 then $0.04; Upscaling 1,000 then $0.025; Virus Detection 1,000 then $0.05.

facts.label: Other AI add-on rates
facts.value: Pricing separately lists optional add-ons such as Smart Crop, Image Tagging, Video Tagging, Image Caption, Facial Detection, Sentiment Analysis and SFW Images with their own fixed fees, unit quotas and overages.

facts.label: Add-on meter independence
facts.value: FAQ says add-on units are independent of plan usage limits; Video Conversion is the exception because it also affects the plan's Transformations quota.

facts.label: Storage meter
facts.value: Pricing FAQ says a file stored in Filestack's own S3 reduces the storage quota by its file size; Free storage is a standing current total and is freed by deleting files.

facts.label: Customer-owned storage billing boundary
facts.value: The FAQ ties storage-quota reduction to Filestack's S3; docs explain customer-owned storage and say files in a connected bucket remain there. Whether all customer-owned storage bytes are excluded from Filestack storage quotas is not stated explicitly.

facts.label: Billing precision
facts.value: Pricing gives GB and per-unit rates but does not state the decimal/binary GB basis, fractional-unit rounding, or a minimum overage block in the plan table.

facts.label: Idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: Not applicable to the comparison field: Filestack provides managed file tasks and workflow executions, but no user-provisioned general compute instance that can sit idle. Task and workflow charges are recorded separately under C13.

facts.label: Bandwidth meter and allowance
facts.value: Bandwidth is not counted for uploads; it is counted when a file is viewed or downloaded. Monthly allowances are Free 1 GB, Start 75 GB, Grow 200 GB and Scale 400 GB.

facts.label: Bandwidth overage
facts.value: After plan allowance, published overage is Start $0.20/GB, Grow $0.15/GB, Scale $0.10/GB; Enterprise custom. Fees are USD under Service Terms.

facts.label: Migration and inbound transfer
facts.value: File migration between sources entails downloading and uploading; pricing FAQ says it consumes bandwidth and counts as new uploads. Standard upload traffic itself is excluded from Filestack bandwidth usage.

facts.label: Regional/network transfer rates
facts.value: No separately itemized inter-region transfer rate or customer-owned-bucket egress rate was found in the pricing, storage docs, CDN docs, or Service Terms checked.

facts.label: Free quota action
facts.value: Free plan is not billed overages under the linked Service Terms; service can be blocked until the next cycle or an upgrade.

facts.label: Paid overage action
facts.value: Start/Grow/Scale can pay listed usage fees or upgrade after included quotas; Enterprise rates are custom. No published hard-dollar ceiling is attached to the overage table.

facts.label: Budget alerts and hard spend caps
facts.value: A user-set monthly spend cap or automatic dollar threshold pause was not found in pricing, billing FAQ, docs index, or Service Terms.

facts.label: Usage visibility
facts.value: Pricing FAQ says the dashboard reports uploads, transformations, storage and bandwidth usage.

facts.label: Free storage allowance
facts.value: Free plan includes 1 GB Filestack storage as a current-size cap; storage does not reset monthly and falls when stored originals are deleted.

facts.label: Start storage allowance and overage
facts.value: Start includes 50 GB; additional Filestack storage is $0.50/GB per month.

facts.label: Grow storage allowance and overage
facts.value: Grow includes 150 GB; additional Filestack storage is $0.375/GB per month.

facts.label: Scale storage allowance and overage
facts.value: Scale includes 350 GB; additional Filestack storage is $0.25/GB per month.

facts.label: Enterprise storage
facts.value: Enterprise storage quota and price are custom; no hot/archive class rates are listed.

facts.label: Upload operation charge
facts.value: Uploads are counted against a monthly file-count allowance; overage is $0.006/upload on Start, $0.005 on Grow and $0.004 on Scale.

facts.label: Read/download charge
facts.value: Filestack does not list a separate per-GET or per-download request price; bytes viewed or downloaded consume bandwidth allowance and then bandwidth overage.

facts.label: List/API request price
facts.value: No separate per-list or general API request tariff was found in pricing, file API reference, FAQ, or Service Terms.

facts.label: Transform operation price
facts.value: General file transformations are counted against monthly transformation quota, then charged at Start $0.0025, Grow $0.002, Scale $0.00125 per transformation. Add-on and video tasks use separate meters.

facts.label: Minimum storage and early deletion
facts.value: No minimum billed file size, minimum storage duration, or early-delete fee was found in pricing, storage docs, File API, or Service Terms.

facts.label: Storage unit basis
facts.value: Public tables use GB, but pricing, billing docs and Service Terms do not define whether this is decimal GB or binary GiB.

facts.label: Public signup and card requirement
facts.value: Public self-service signup is available. Free is $0, stays active, and does not require a credit card; email confirmation is required to obtain the API key.

facts.label: Signup information and email restrictions
facts.value: Free signup asks for name, email, country and password. The FAQ says Yahoo addresses are automatically denied for security reasons.

facts.label: Country/account eligibility
facts.value: A country-by-country eligibility rule was not found in the Free signup, pricing, docs, FAQ, privacy, or Service Terms pages checked.

facts.label: Commercial use and resale
facts.value: The Service Terms allow use in a revenue-generating application but prohibit reselling Filestack as a stand-alone service.

facts.label: Trial length
facts.value: Start/Grow/Scale cards have a “Start Free Trial” button, but current pricing, signup, docs and linked Service Terms do not state a current trial length. An official old blog comparison says 21 days, but does not establish the current offer.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: Researcher classification: hosted file upload, processing and delivery API, with bundled file storage. It also offers workflows and AI/document tasks. It is not presented as a general-purpose S3-compatible object-storage endpoint.

facts.label: Included file service
facts.value: File Picker, upload APIs, file handles, transformations, storage destinations, CDN delivery, and file management APIs are documented parts of the service.

facts.label: Storage options
facts.value: Filestack stores files in its internally managed S3 by default; it documents integrations for customer-owned S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure, Dropbox, and Rackspace.

facts.label: Processing services
facts.value: URL-based file/image/document transformations are offered. The plans also list OCR, document detection, image enhancement/upscaling, and virus detection with individual monthly units and overage prices on paid plans.

facts.label: Workflows and other backend features
facts.value: Workflows automate file-processing tasks and return results through status calls or webhooks. Filestack is not documented as providing a database, user-auth system, or general-purpose app server.

facts.label: API and upload protocols
facts.value: HTTPS REST APIs and URL-based Processing API are documented. The API endpoint is Filestack's own; no S3-compatible endpoint is documented for Filestack-managed storage.

facts.label: SDKs and client platforms
facts.value: Official SDK docs cover Android, Angular, Go, iOS, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Python, React, Ruby and Swift; other HTTP-capable clients can use REST.

facts.label: Public access default
facts.value: Security page says uploads and delivery are open until application security is enabled; then every request must carry a signature.

facts.label: Signed policies and file scoping
facts.value: Policies can expire and restrict calls, file handle, upload path, and maximum file size; app secret signing stays server-side.

facts.label: Domain and origin controls
facts.value: Domain whitelists can restrict embedding by Origin and Referer; custom CNAME is offered as a paid add-on on Start/Grow/Scale.

facts.label: Encryption and platform controls
facts.value: Filestack states TLS 1.2 for transfer, AES-256 at rest and AWS KMS key management. The DPA lists encryption and access-control measures; this is vendor-published security information, not an independent certification result.

facts.label: Customer-owned S3 access
facts.value: S3 storage setup requires customer bucket permissions for Filestack upload/write tasks; docs describe IAM and CORS setup.

facts.label: Maximum upload size by plan
facts.value: Maximum file sizes: Free 20 MB, Start 1 GB, Grow 2 GB, Scale 5 GB, Enterprise custom.

facts.label: Multipart and resumable uploads
facts.value: Upload API documents multipart upload; current docs and pricing list resumable uploads. File Picker 4.0 documents pause/resume/cancel controls.

facts.label: File types
facts.value: Product pages say any file type is supported, with specialized processing support depending on file type and plan.

facts.label: Failed attempts and repeat uploads
facts.value: File Upload FAQ says failed upload attempts do not consume upload allowance and a re-upload counts as a new upload. The special case of overwriting an existing handle is unclear; see C13.

facts.label: Batch file count
facts.value: Multi-file uploads are billed per file, not per picker session or batch.

facts.label: Multipage PDFs and animated files
facts.value: Pricing FAQ says multipage PDFs and animated files are counted “per action” and directs users to docs/support for case-specific details; exact page/frame rules are not published there.

facts.label: S3 API compatibility
facts.value: Filestack-managed files use Filestack File/Processing APIs. Docs describe writing to a customer's S3 bucket, but no general S3-compatible endpoint or full S3 operation matrix for Filestack is published.

facts.label: Integrated CDN
facts.value: Integrated CDN is included on Free, Start, Grow and Scale; Enterprise custom plan.

facts.label: Cache behavior
facts.value: Each unique Filestack URL is cached for a default 30 days; the content is fetched again on a later request after expiry. Cache can be bypassed or changed, and low-traffic cache entries can be purged earlier.

facts.label: Private delivery controls
facts.value: Delivery is open until application security is enabled; signed policy URLs then restrict expiry and permitted calls. Domain whitelist supports Origin/Referer restrictions.

facts.label: Custom domain
facts.value: Custom CNAME is listed as a $79/month add-on on Start, Grow and Scale; Enterprise pricing is custom.

facts.label: Customer storage alias
facts.value: Storage Aliases let Scale/Enterprise use their own storage as a source for transformations, including files not uploaded through Filestack. Pricing page does not include Storage Aliases on Free, Start or Grow.

facts.label: Public/private bucket control
facts.value: Filestack request access can be constrained with signed policy; connected S3 access and public/private bucket behavior also depends on the customer's own storage configuration. A universal default bucket ACL for every destination was not established.

facts.label: Default data location
facts.value: Filestack says its infrastructure runs on AWS us-east-1 and default file storage is in Northern Virginia, USA.

facts.label: Customer-selected data location
facts.value: Customer-owned S3 can be in any region, and Filestack says stored files follow that bucket. Current security page also lists own-bucket storage as the path to file residency choice.

facts.label: Processing locations
facts.value: Security page lists processing in the US (hosting/storage/delivery/scanning), Germany (document transformations), Canada (image enhancement), Australia (project management/status), and New Zealand (invoicing).

facts.label: Regional residency controls
facts.value: Filestack-managed files default to US storage; a customer can bring their own S3 bucket in another region. No managed-region selection or data-localization guarantee per paid plan was found.

facts.label: File export and download
facts.value: File API supports downloading files by handle; docs expose file metadata and storage location. Terms make customers responsible for exporting content before contract expiration.

facts.label: File listing in the Developer Portal
facts.value: Older FAQ says Filestack does not directly provide a list of uploaded files; current Quick Start says the Developer Portal Assets section can search all files for an application. Whether this provides a full exportable inventory is not stated.

facts.label: Bulk export
facts.value: A one-click bulk export for all application files was not found in the File API, storage docs, current Quick Start, FAQ, or terms.

facts.label: Deleting files
facts.value: File API provides a signed DELETE by handle. Its skip_storage option removes the Filestack record but leaves the object in the configured storage container.

facts.label: File-retention and deletion timing
facts.value: Service Terms say Filestack URLs are not intended to survive indefinitely and will be maintained for a reasonable period; on termination for breach, content is retained at least 15 days, then may be destroyed. No exact purge time for normal cancellation or successful file deletion was found.

facts.label: Personal-data retention
facts.value: Idera's Privacy Notice says personal data may be retained for a reasonable period after an account ends and for legal, security, audit or dispute needs; it gives no fixed deletion interval. This covers personal data, not a service-file object-retention schedule.

facts.label: Backups and customer duty
facts.value: Service Terms require customers to make and securely retain their own backups. The published Security page describes daily backups on a seven-day window but does not clearly say that this is a recoverable backup of every customer's file object.

facts.label: Service backup statement
facts.value: Security page says daily backups on a seven-day window and cross-region database replication, but does not identify whether every customer file object is included.

facts.label: File versioning and undelete
facts.value: No customer-facing object version history, retention lock, or undelete window was found in File API, storage docs, pricing, or terms.

facts.label: Recovery responsibility
facts.value: Service Terms require customers to maintain their own backups; exact Filestack recovery point, restore time, customer-file restore path and file-level backup exclusion are not published.

facts.label: Identity and old names
facts.value: Filestack is the current product name and official site. No different former product name was established in the current About or docs pages.

facts.label: Identity and ownership
facts.value: Idera, Inc. acquired Filestack, Inc. in January 2022; Idera's current Brands page lists Filestack under Developer Tools. The public Service Terms still name Filestack, Inc. as contracting party.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: Hosted SaaS only in the public product offer. The File Uploader/API is licensed for use with the service; no self-hosted server edition or open-source product license is described in the official docs or terms index.

facts.label: Self-hosting
facts.value: No public self-host deployment instructions or self-hosted Filestack server license were found in the docs index, pricing page, product overview, or Service Terms.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: Active hosted offer: current public pricing, Free signup, 2026 docs and blog updates, and an operational status page were found.

facts.label: Parent-company change
facts.value: Idera acquisition is the known ownership change.

facts.label: Shutdown or sunset notice search
facts.value: No Filestack service shutdown or sunset announcement was found in the Filestack blog, Press page, Idera News, pricing page, docs changelog, or status page. Current blog items include Workflows 2.0 (November 1, 2026) and a dashboard update (November 5, 2026).

facts.label: Vendor location
facts.value: Filestack's About page says it is headquartered in San Antonio, Texas, USA. Idera's current legal page lists its headquarters in Austin, Texas.

facts.label: Markets served
facts.value: Filestack says it is used by developers around the world and describes customer use across several industries; no complete country eligibility or served-market list was found.

facts.label: Support path
facts.value: Free includes community support; Start/Grow/Scale pricing includes Standard Support; Platinum Support is a paid add-on. The linked Service Terms say all plans receive documentation and chat/ticket responses during weekday support hours, creating a support-scope conflict for Free.

facts.label: SLA and availability promise
facts.value: Standard Service Terms promise commercially reasonable availability, not a numeric uptime SLA. They say service-level commitments require an explicit plan/order; no public standard-plan percentage was found.

facts.label: Public status
facts.value: Status page lists API, Conversions, Developer Portal, Client/Picker, Support and Uploads as Operational.

apps.line: Google backend: Firestore, auth, storage, functions and hosting.

facts.label: Free offer type
facts.value: Spark is recurring no-cost hosted usage, not trial credit. Blaze retains eligible no-cost quotas and bills excess. SQL Connect has separate time-limited database trials.

facts.label: Firestore Standard free limits
facts.value: One qualifying database/project: 1 GiB stored, 50,000 reads/day, 20,000 writes/day, 20,000 deletes/day and 10 GiB outbound/month. Daily operation quotas reset around midnight Pacific.

facts.label: Firestore free database eligibility conflict
facts.value: Firebase billing docs give free quota to the first database regardless of ID. Google Cloud pricing says named non-default databases do not qualify.

facts.label: Firestore Enterprise allowances
facts.value: Pricing page: 1 GiB storage, 10 GiB egress/month; daily 50,000 read units, 40,000 write units and 50,000 realtime update units. Enterprise docs label free storage 1GB instead.

facts.label: Realtime Database free limits
facts.value: Spark: 1 GB database storage, 10 GB downloads/month, 100 concurrent connections and one database. Blaze permits 200,000 connections/database and multiple databases.

facts.label: Realtime Database Blaze allowance conflict
facts.value: Pricing page: 360 MB downloaded/day, described as roughly 10 GB/month. Realtime Database billing guide: 10 GB/month retained on Blaze.

facts.label: Cloud Storage recurring allowance
facts.value: Blaze new buckets: 5 GB-month storage, 5,000 Class A and 50,000 Class B operations/month; 100 GB outbound from North America except China/Australia. Free-tier regions: us-central1/us-east1/us-west1, combined.

facts.label: Spark Storage documentation conflict
facts.value: General pricing-plan guide still lists Cloud Storage among Spark quota products; current pricing and Storage FAQ say Blaze is required for all bucket access.

facts.label: Authentication limits
facts.value: Identity Platform pricing includes 50,000 non-SAML/OIDC MAU and 50 SAML/OIDC MAU. Instrumentless Spark Identity Platform also has daily active-user caps: 3,000 tier 1 and 2 tier 2. Phone SMS is Blaze-only and priced by destination.

facts.label: Projects and apps
facts.value: Spark project creation quota is usually about 5–10 per Google account; Blaze quota can increase with a billing account. Firebase normally restricts each project to 30 registered apps.

facts.label: SQL Connect trial resources
facts.value: Spark: one trial database/project for 90 days, 330 MiB/day egress. Blaze: one default trial instance/project, up to five trial projects/billing account, for three months. Default trial configuration: db-f1-micro, 1 vCPU, 10 GB storage and 628.74 MB RAM.

facts.label: SQL trial operation quota conflict
facts.value: Spark trial pricing table says 8,300K operations/day; detailed SQL pricing says 8,300 operations/day and approximately 8,000/day in its trial section.

facts.label: Ordinary idle project retention
facts.value: A universal inactivity sleep/automatic deletion interval for ordinary Spark Firestore/Realtime Database projects was not found.

facts.label: SQL Connect trial expiry
facts.value: Spark database trial lasts 90 days, then archives the instance if not upgraded; deletion follows another 90 days without upgrade. Blaze trial converts to paid Cloud SQL pricing after three months.

facts.label: Least paid commitment
facts.value: Blaze is usage billing without a Firebase subscription/seat fee shown. A billing account/payment method is required even where the billable workload stays in a recurring allowance.

facts.label: SQL Connect paid floor
facts.value: SQL Connect API: 250,000 operations/month included, then USD $0.90/million. Cloud SQL is separately billed after trial, advertised starting as low as $9.37/month, depending on region/configuration.

facts.label: Currency and taxes
facts.value: Google Cloud price tables specify USD; local currency SKUs apply if billed otherwise. Customer is responsible for applicable taxes under the relevant agreements.

facts.label: Firestore Standard operation rates
facts.value: Iowa/us-central1 on-demand: reads USD $0.03/100,000 documents; writes $0.09/100,000; deletes/TTL deletes $0.01/100,000 beyond applicable quotas.

facts.label: Firestore Standard storage and recovery rates
facts.value: Iowa hourly display: database/PITR USD $0.000205479/GiB-hour; backups $0.000041096/GiB-hour. Restore/clone $0.20/GiB.

facts.label: Firestore query meters
facts.value: Queries charge at least one document read; ordinary billable index scans add one read per up-to-1,000 entries, kNN scans one per up-to-100. Security-rule lookups and listener changes/reconnects can add reads.

facts.label: Firestore Enterprise meters
facts.value: Iowa: USD $0.05/million read units (4 KiB); $0.26/million write units (1 KiB, including index writes/deletes); realtime updates $0.30/million units. Storage shown $0.00032/GiB-hour in Firebase comparison.

facts.label: Realtime Database pricing
facts.value: Storage USD $5/GB-month, evaluated daily; downloaded traffic $1/GB after applicable allowance. Protocol, connection/TLS overhead and denied operations can contribute billable traffic.

facts.label: Other product dependencies
facts.value: Cloud Functions can incur Cloud Build, Artifact Registry, Logging, Secret Manager and event/queue charges. SQL Connect adds Cloud SQL and optional Vertex AI embeddings. Hosting/App Hosting have their own storage/transfer/runtime meters.

facts.label: Scale to zero
facts.value: Functions default to autoscaling, including zero instances at low traffic. Configured minimum instances stay warm and incur idle charges. Firestore/Realtime Database retain stored-data charges when unused.

facts.label: SQL idle commitment
facts.value: SQL Connect API inactivity does not remove its separately provisioned Cloud SQL instance bill after trial. Its management guide supports stopping/restarting Cloud SQL, but no Firebase-wide automatic scale-to-zero promise was found.

facts.label: Firestore network rates
facts.value: 10 GiB/month no-cost outbound; Iowa-to-normal worldwide internet destinations then USD $0.12/GiB for the next tier. Ingress free. China/Australia and certain origin/destination combinations have separate tiers.

facts.label: File transfer rates
facts.value: New buckets follow Cloud Storage: ingress free; normal worldwide internet egress USD $0.12/GiB through first 10 TiB, then $0.11/$0.08 at higher tiers. China/Australia cost more; eligible US free-tier allowance is separate.

facts.label: Legacy file transfer
facts.value: Legacy appspot.com default buckets retain 1 GB/day downloads included on Blaze, then $0.12/GB. New firebasestorage.app buckets follow the Cloud Storage allowance and rates instead.

facts.label: Spark and Blaze quota behavior
facts.value: Spark shuts off an affected product when its applicable no-cost quota is exceeded; Blaze bills overages. Daily Firestore quotas and SQL trial limits require their product-specific reset rules.

facts.label: Budget alerts
facts.value: Budget alerts notify; they do not stop usage or charges. Disabling billing via programmatic notifications is a separate intervention that can interrupt multiple services.

facts.label: Spend caps
facts.value: Preview spend caps cover Firebase AI Logic, App Hosting, Cloud Functions and Extensions via underlying cloud services. At 100%, new usage pauses for the month; reporting can lag minutes and overshoot is billed.

facts.label: Cap restart and exclusions
facts.value: Caps reset next month; lifting a cap resumes uncapped usage for the month unless reconfigured. Coverage follows the underlying service, not every build/storage/logging dependency of a Firebase feature.

facts.label: Firestore Standard limits
facts.value: Document 1 MiB; API request 10 MiB; transaction 270 seconds with 60-second idle expiration. Default project database limit 100. Composite index quota 200 without billing, 1,000 with billing.

facts.label: Firestore Enterprise limits
facts.value: Document 16 MiB; query memory 128 MiB; transaction 270 seconds with 60-second idle expiration; normally 1,000 indexes/database and 100 databases/project.

facts.label: Realtime Database limits
facts.value: Spark 100 or Blaze 200,000 simultaneous connections/database. Single response 256 MB; single write 16 MB through SDK or 256 MB REST. Sustained >1,000 writes/second can be limited.

facts.label: SQL Connect request capacity
facts.value: GraphQL quota 24,000 requests/minute/project/region. Cloud SQL connection/memory capacity depends on the instance; the guide links Cloud SQL quotas rather than giving one platform-wide connection count.

facts.label: New-bucket storage prices
facts.value: Iowa regional hourly USD rates/GiB-hour: Standard $0.000027397; Nearline $0.000013699; Coldline $0.000005479; Archive $0.000001644. Metadata, noncurrent and soft-deleted copies also consume storage.

facts.label: Legacy default-bucket storage
facts.value: Legacy appspot.com default bucket on Blaze retains 5 GB free, then $0.026/GB. New bucket rates/allowances are different.

facts.label: New-bucket requests and retrieval
facts.value: Regional flat-namespace Standard: USD $0.005/1,000 Class A; $0.0004/1,000 Class B. Upload/list are generally A; reads/metadata generally B; deletes free operations. Resumable JSON upload counts once.

facts.label: Archive retrieval and image processing
facts.value: Retrieval USD/GiB: Standard $0, Nearline $0.01, Coldline $0.02, Archive $0.05, in addition to applicable requests/egress. Image processing is separate function/provider work, not a storage retrieval tariff.

facts.label: Legacy request prices
facts.value: appspot.com: 20,000 uploads/day then $0.05/10,000; 50,000 downloads/day then $0.004/10,000, on Blaze.

facts.label: Minimum size and retention
facts.value: Cloud Storage has no minimum object size. Standard has no minimum duration; Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90 days, Archive 365 days. Early delete/replace/move can bill the remaining minimum duration.

facts.label: Firestore vector limits
facts.value: Maximum embedding dimension 2,048; Standard kNN result limit 1,000. Supported vector-search clients: Python, Node.js, Go, Java. No realtime snapshot listeners for vector queries.

facts.label: Billed vector representation
facts.value: Firestore storage calculation counts vectors as 8 bytes/dimension, before field names, document names, document overhead and indexes.

facts.label: Embedding charges
facts.value: Firestore does not generate embeddings; obtain them externally. SQL Connect can call Vertex AI via _embed/embedding queries, including in local development, and incurs Vertex AI usage charges.

facts.label: Generation-specific runtime limits
facts.value: 2nd gen: HTTP/callable up to 3,600 seconds, task/scheduled up to 1,800, other event functions 540. 1st gen limit 540 seconds. Memory maxima: 8 GiB first gen, 32 GiB second gen.

facts.label: CPU/concurrency/scaling
facts.value: 2nd gen defaults to 1 CPU through 2 GB memory. Fractional CPU is configurable; CPU below 1 disables per-instance concurrency beyond 1. Default concurrency otherwise 80, maximum 1,000; min/max instances configurable.

facts.label: Second-gen runtime price
facts.value: Cloud Run request-based Iowa on-demand: USD $0.000024/vCPU-second active; $0.0000025/GiB-second; $0.40/million requests. Rounded up to 100 ms; monthly free 180,000 vCPU-seconds, 360,000 GiB-seconds and 2M requests, shared by billing account.

facts.label: Queue/schedule charges
facts.value: Cloud Tasks first 1M operations/month/account free, then USD $0.40/million; operations chunked by 32 KB and include create/push attempts. Scheduler USD $0.10/job/month, first 3 jobs/Google account free.

facts.label: Signup and commercial use
facts.value: Spark requires no payment method. Blaze requires a linked Cloud Billing account/payment method. Firebase terms require use related to trade/business/craft/profession; Paid Services Agreement specifies business, not consumer, use.

facts.label: Country/account eligibility
facts.value: A complete Firebase-specific signup country/territory eligibility list was not found. Regional contracting entities are published but do not prove availability in every country.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: Researcher classification: managed backend platform; document database, realtime JSON database, PostgreSQL API, auth, files, functions, jobs and frontend hosting as secondary roles.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Firestore, Realtime Database, SQL Connect, Authentication, Cloud Storage, Cloud Functions, Hosting/App Hosting, App Check and messaging. SQL Connect adds a separate Cloud SQL dependency.

facts.label: Jobs and external services
facts.value: Task queue functions use Cloud Tasks; scheduled functions use Cloud Scheduler. Functions run managed code; queues/schedules and underlying cloud resources have separate charges.

facts.label: Client and server connections
facts.value: Client SDKs cover Apple, Android, web, Flutter, Unity and C++ with product-specific support. Admin SDKs cover Node.js, Java, Python, Go and C#. Realtime Database also provides REST.

facts.label: SQL and Enterprise connections
facts.value: SQL Connect exposes predefined GraphQL queries/mutations through generated Kotlin, iOS, Flutter and web SDKs; privileged direct SQL access requires Cloud SQL/PostgreSQL permissions. Firestore Enterprise separately offers Native or MongoDB-compatible modes.

facts.label: Hosted function runtimes
facts.value: Functions documentation lists Node.js 20/22 and Python 3.10/3.11 configuration; JavaScript/TypeScript and Python SDKs. Node.js 18 is deprecated; Dart SDK is experimental.

facts.label: Firestore permissions
facts.value: Mobile/web clients are checked by Security Rules; use Authentication and record-specific authorization. Server SDKs bypass these rules and use Google credentials/IAM.

facts.label: File access and secrets
facts.value: Cloud Storage Security Rules support per-user authorization, file-size/type validation and default authenticated access. Functions bind Secret Manager secrets; service accounts, private invoker and ingress/VPC options are configurable.

facts.label: Firestore engine/query model
facts.value: Standard: document database with Core operations and indexes. Enterprise: Native Core/Pipeline operations or a separately selected MongoDB-compatible mode; optional/custom indexes and MQL/BSON support in that mode.

facts.label: Realtime and SQL engines
facts.value: Realtime Database stores a JSON tree with SDK/REST access. SQL Connect maps GraphQL schema and predefined operations onto a managed Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database.

facts.label: Firestore transactions
facts.value: Atomic multi-document transactions and batched writes; transactions provide serializable isolation by commit time. Contention is retried finitely and can still fail.

facts.label: Realtime Database atomicity
facts.value: Multi-location update is atomic. runTransaction retries against updated data on conflict until accepted or aborted. Local events fire before server acknowledgement.

facts.label: SQL Connect transaction opt-in
facts.value: @transaction makes a mutation fully succeed or roll back, including multiple fields/substeps. Without it, root fields execute sequentially and partial errors can leave successful earlier effects.

facts.label: Development environments
facts.value: Firebase recommends a separate project per environment. Local emulators isolate supported tests; their data/security/performance behavior is not a production replica.

facts.label: Clones and branch semantics
facts.value: Firestore PITR supports cloning to a new database at an earlier timestamp. Copy-on-write database branch semantics and a branch-specific fee were not established.

facts.label: Firestore replication/failover
facts.value: Regional data is replicated across zones. Multi-region data spans read/write and witness regions and can remain served after a region loss. No user-created replica is required for the published topology.

facts.label: Firestore offline sync
facts.value: Android/Apple persistent cache enabled by default; web disabled by default, with Chrome/Safari/Firefox support. Cached reads/writes/listens sync on reconnection; changes to the same document use last-write-wins.

facts.label: Realtime offline behavior
facts.value: Realtime SDKs support local events/presence/reconnect. Android disk persistence survives app restarts for cached data and queued writes; queued transactions are not persisted across restarts, even with persistence enabled.

facts.label: Specialized indexes and search
facts.value: Firestore Standard supports single-field/composite and vector indexes. Enterprise adds custom/unique index options and native text-search indexes with Pipeline search/documentMatches. SQL Connect vector search uses pgvector.

facts.label: File size and upload methods
facts.value: Underlying Cloud Storage maximum object 5 TiB, including composed/resumable/multipart objects. Firebase web SDK supports resumable uploads with pause, resume and cancel.

facts.label: Multipart constraints
facts.value: Cloud Storage XML multipart: up to 10,000 parts; assembled object must still fit 5 TiB. Multipart and Firebase SDK resumable protocols are distinct methods.

facts.label: Storage API compatibility
facts.value: Firebase SDK plus underlying Google Cloud Storage JSON/XML/gRPC APIs. XML API interoperates with some S3 tools via storage.googleapis.com and HMAC/V4 credentials; it is partial interoperability, not complete S3 parity.

facts.label: Private files and direct downloads
facts.value: Storage rules can authorize by request.auth.uid and validate uploads. SDK getDownloadURL/direct byte download are documented; use the appropriate auth/rules path for app access.

facts.label: Expiring signed URLs
facts.value: Underlying GCS signed URLs grant bearer access until expiry/key rotation; V4 expiry maximum 604,800 seconds (7 days). They use XML API endpoints.

facts.label: CDN/custom domain scope
facts.value: Firebase Hosting includes custom domain/SSL with its own storage and transfer limits. Cloud CDN integration changes GCS transfer billing and can add cache-fill charges.

facts.label: Similarity and filters
facts.value: Firestore kNN offers Euclidean, cosine and dot-product distances, pre-filtering with a suitable composite vector index and distance thresholds. Enterprise separately offers indexed text search.

facts.label: Hybrid ranking uncertainty
facts.value: A single native combined keyword/vector fusion/reranking contract was not established in the checked Firestore and SQL Connect guides. Separate text, vector and filtering operations are documented.

facts.label: Job execution and languages
facts.value: Managed Cloud Functions with Node.js/JavaScript/TypeScript or Python. Task functions dispatch from Cloud Tasks; onSchedule functions use Cloud Scheduler. Spark cannot deploy these paid cloud functions.

facts.label: Event delivery/retries
facts.value: Event-driven functions provide at-least-once delivery. Retry-on-failure is disabled by default; enabled retry windows are 24 hours second gen, 7 days first gen. Functions must handle duplicates/idempotency.

facts.label: Task queues and ordering
facts.value: Task queues configure retry/backoff and dispatch concurrency. Cloud Tasks has no execution-order guarantee; duplicate executions can happen. Named-task deduplication persists up to 24 hours after deletion.

facts.label: Dead-letter and failure routing
facts.value: Retry guide describes custom HTTP + Pub/Sub subscriptions to configure dead-letter topics and delivery policies. A base Firebase task-function automatic dead-letter queue/replay contract was not found.

facts.label: Queue retention/payload
facts.value: Cloud Tasks: maximum task 1 MiB, retention 31 days from creation, schedule time up to 30 days ahead. Maximum dispatch rate 500 tasks/second/queue; inactive after 30 days without calls or dispatches.

facts.label: Recurring schedules
facts.value: onSchedule accepts cron/App Engine schedule syntax. Cloud Scheduler supports timezone selection. Overlapping function invocations are possible, so app logic must handle concurrent repeats.

facts.label: Logs and run investigation
facts.value: Functions logs use Cloud Logging; Firebase/Google Cloud console and CLI expose them. Cloud Logging project _Default bucket retains 30 days by default, configurable 1–3,650 days; _Required bucket retains 400 days.

facts.label: Longer history/export and replay
facts.value: Log routing/sinks can send records to external storage/analytics and incur charges. Cloud Tasks runTask supports manual debugging, but a log record is not a durable replayable task after successful removal/expiry.

facts.label: Production self-host requirements
facts.value: Not applicable to a production self-host edition: Firebase explicitly says not to run Local Emulator Suite as a production self-hosted service.

facts.label: Location scope
facts.value: No global project location setting. Firestore, Realtime Database, Storage buckets, SQL Connect and Functions select locations independently, subject to documented legacy dependencies.

facts.label: Firestore regions and replicas
facts.value: Regional choices include us-central1 and listed global regions; multi-regions eur3, nam5, nam7. Regional data spans zones; multi-regions have read/write and witness regions. Location cannot change after provisioning.

facts.label: Realtime Database location
facts.value: us-central1 (Iowa), europe-west1 (Belgium), asia-southeast1 (Singapore). Each instance has a fixed location; Blaze can create multiple instances in different locations.

facts.label: Workers, SQL and backups
facts.value: Functions default to us-central1 unless specified. SQL Connect service and its Cloud SQL instance must share a supported region. Firestore scheduled backups remain in the database location.

facts.label: Auth and policy location
facts.value: Firebase Authentication operates only in US data centers. For products without location selection, Google can process/store data where it or agents have facilities.

facts.label: Firestore export
facts.value: Blaze managed export/import uses Cloud Storage and gcloud/REST/RPC; can move all documents or collection groups between databases. Export charges document reads plus storage/transfer; it is not a general JSON dump.

facts.label: Other data export
facts.value: Realtime Database backups export JSON data/rules, optionally gzip. Auth CLI exports CSV/JSON with scrypt-password limitations. Cloud SQL supports SQL dump/CSV exports; serverless offloaded exports cost extra.

facts.label: Deletion and retention
facts.value: Project deletion takes 30 days in the Firebase FAQ. Applicable data-processing terms allow up to 180 days for unrecoverable customer deletion instructions, with legal exceptions; term-end deletion has an up-to-30-day recovery period first.

facts.label: Authentication data deletion
facts.value: Privacy page says Auth keeps non-IP authentication data until user deletion, then removes it from live/backup systems within 180 days. Logged IPs remain for a few weeks.

facts.label: Firestore scheduled backups
facts.value: Blaze daily and/or weekly backups; each schedule can retain backups up to 14 weeks. Backups contain database data/index configurations, exclude TTL policies and remain in the database location.

facts.label: Firestore PITR
facts.value: Paid, disabled by default; retains up to 7 days at one-version-per-minute granularity. Recover selected data or clone/export into a new database. PITR has a minimum of up to one day of storage billing.

facts.label: Firestore recovery charges/scope
facts.value: Backup capacity, PITR capacity, restore and clone are separately charged, without free quota. Database backups do not bundle Storage file objects, Auth accounts, function source or all project settings.

facts.label: Realtime Database backups
facts.value: Blaze supports daily JSON backups of data and Security Rules into Cloud Storage, manual snapshots and optional gzip. Optional 30-day bucket lifecycle deletes older backups; storage charges remain.

facts.label: SQL recovery scope
facts.value: SQL Connect and Cloud SQL are administered separately; the service guide sends PostgreSQL backup administration to Cloud SQL. Exact recovery retention, HA and price require the chosen Cloud SQL configuration.

facts.label: Soft delete recovery
facts.value: Compatible GCS buckets default to 7-day soft-delete retention; configurable 7–90 days, or 0 to disable. Soft-deleted files/buckets can be restored during retention and continue storage billing.

facts.label: Versions and retention locks
facts.value: GCS Object Versioning retains noncurrent object versions until removed; it does not protect bucket deletion by itself. Bucket Lock can make a retention policy irreversible and prevent early deletion/replacement.

facts.label: Identity and old names
facts.value: Firebase, Google backend services at firebase.google.com. Firestore, Realtime Database and SQL Connect are distinct database products in the bundle.

facts.label: Component naming
facts.value: Older Data Connect pricing URL redirects to Firebase SQL Connect pricing. Current service/SDK docs use SQL Connect; some CLI commands retain dataconnect.

facts.label: SDK license

facts.value: Firestore formal SLA: multi-region 99.999%; regional 99.99% except Stockholm regional 99.95%. Hosting/Realtime Database SLA: 99.95%. Credits depend on paid affected fees, exclusions and claim conditions.

facts.value: Garage is free software under AGPLv3, not a hosted free tier or time-limited trial.

facts.value: Deuxfleurs’ website describes a voluntary contribution price for its hosted services, but that is not a Garage software license or a Garage managed plan.

facts.label: free limits
facts.value: Garage does not publish one universal maximum cluster storage quota; usable capacity depends on node disks, assigned capacity, replication, and metadata overhead.

facts.label: free limits
facts.value: A three-copy layout uses three replicas for each replicated data block before compression or deduplication.

facts.label: inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: Hosted idle-project pause, expiry, and restore rules do not apply to a user-run Garage cluster.

facts.label: billing meters

facts.label: idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: Managed idle compute, scale-to-zero billing, and wake behavior do not apply to self-hosted Garage. Stopping the process is an operator action and can interrupt service.

facts.label: data transfer costs
facts.value: Garage publishes no vendor egress tariff or included transfer allowance. Internet, inter-node, or cross-region network bills come from the operator’s host or network provider.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: Hosted quota overages, budget caps, and billing alerts do not apply. Hardware capacity and any provider account controls must be managed outside Garage.

facts.label: storage prices
facts.value: Vendor hot/archive storage rates and monthly storage allowances do not apply to self-hosted Garage. The operator supplies the object disks.

facts.label: file request and retrieval prices

facts.label: minimum storage and early deletion
facts.value: Vendor capacity floors, minimum object sizes, minimum retention periods, and early-delete fees do not apply to self-hosted Garage.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: The AGPLv3 license governs copying and use of the software; the product pages reviewed do not add a Garage-specific commercial-use signup restriction.

facts.label: primary type and other roles
facts.value: Primary type: self-hosted S3-compatible distributed object and file storage. This is our directory classification, based on Garage's stated purpose.

facts.label: primary type and other roles
facts.value: Secondary roles: multi-site replication, static website serving from buckets, and an experimental key/value API.

facts.label: included backend services

facts.value: Garage can serve a bucket as a static website. Website serving supports an index document and an error document, but not dynamic languages or directory listing.

facts.value: K2V is an experimental bulk key/value API for small key/value records; it is not described as a general SQL database.

facts.label: included backend services

facts.value: Garage supports S3 Signature V4. General configuration and compatibility docs describe path-style and virtual-host URLs, while the Nextcloud integration guide says Garage supports only path-style URLs.

facts.value: The docs show the Python MinIO SDK connecting to Garage’s S3 endpoint. The Python page’s boto3 section is marked “Coming soon,” so it is not counted as a Garage-verified boto3 example.

facts.value: The Go page lists MinIO Go and AWS SDK Go references but marks its S3 guide “Coming soon.”

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: S3 access keys are created by the operator, then granted read, write, or owner permissions for selected buckets. A bucket is not accessible to a key until permission is granted.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Garage does not implement AWS bucket policies or normal S3 ACLs; it uses its own per-key/per-bucket permission model.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: The admin API uses bearer tokens. User-defined tokens can be limited to selected calls and can have an expiry date; the documentation discourages relying on a single master token.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Garage’s S3 API does not provide TLS by itself in the documented deployment. The docs show adding a TLS reverse proxy or using an encrypted overlay network.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Data is stored in plaintext on disk unless the operator uses encrypted disks or client-provided SSE-C keys. Garage does not implement SSE-S3-style automatic server encryption.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: The RPC secret protects inter-node communication identity; the RPC port must be reachable between cluster nodes and should not be exposed as an unprotected public app endpoint.

facts.label: upload and file limits

facts.value: With the default LMDB metadata engine, S3 object keys are limited to 479 bytes; this is not a 479-character limit and other configured metadata engines may have different constraints.

facts.label: upload and file limits
facts.value: The default object block size is 1 MiB. Docs recommend considering 10 MiB for large files on fast node networks; block size is a tuning setting, not an object-size quota.

facts.value: No file extension or MIME-type allowlist is stated in the reviewed upload documentation.

facts.label: delivery and private files

facts.value: Product site lists Linux support, x86_64 CPUs from the last 10 years or ARMv7/ARMv8, 1 GB RAM, at least 16 GB disk, and network latency of 200 ms or less with at least 50 Mbps.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Garage ships as a single dependency-free Linux binary and can also run in Docker; the operator must mount persistent metadata and data directories or container termination can wipe the instance.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: For production cluster mode, the deployment guide recommends at least three nodes; each needs storage and direct network reachability to peers, including an appropriate VPN or IPv6 setup if behind NAT.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The operator manages persistent metadata, data, and snapshots. The LMDB metadata map defaults to 1 TiB on 64-bit machines and 1 GiB on 32-bit machines; 32-bit LMDB is not recommended for large databases.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Garage supports LMDB (the default), SQLite, and experimental Fjall metadata engines; the documentation says LMDB is the most tested.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Operators must keep persistent volumes, cluster configuration, RPC secrets, tokens, upgrades, and recovery procedures safe; Garage’s upgrade guide requires coordinated cluster maintenance.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Automatic metadata snapshots can be configured; Garage keeps the two most recent snapshots. They protect metadata recovery, not a separate copy of every object.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Garage is designed for modest hardware and Internet links; the cluster guide recommends at least three nodes for three-way redundancy.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The default block_ram_buffer_max is 256 MiB but is not a hard process-memory ceiling; concurrent large requests use additional buffers.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Monitoring endpoints expose Prometheus metrics and optionally OpenTelemetry traces; the operator selects and retains the monitoring backend.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Published limitations include performance issues with very large objects and object counts, non-sharded bucket metadata, and uneven capacity distribution beyond roughly 10 × the replication factor in node count.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Published S3 feature gaps include no object versioning, normal S3 bucket-policy/ACL system, Object Lock, or automatic server-side encryption.

facts.label: regions and data location
facts.value: Garage has no vendor region catalogue. The operator chooses node locations and assigns them to zones in the cluster layout.

facts.label: regions and data location
facts.value: Garage recommends placing three replicas in separate physical zones for its three-way resilience mode. The zone labels must match actual machine locations.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Garage uses the S3 object API, so S3 clients and backup programs can read objects from a cluster. The project documents tools including restic and rclone as integrations.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Garage cluster replication is not a substitute for a separate backup. The docs describe using restic and other external backup tools.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: A Garage-account closure, vendor-held purge schedule, or account export fee does not apply to the self-hosted instance. The operator deletes local data and any copies or backups.

facts.label: file recovery and protection
facts.value: Recommended three-way replication places three copies across zones. With nodes in at least three zones, the recovery guide says the cluster remains fully functional if failures are confined to one zone and avoids data loss if failures span at most two zones.

facts.label: file recovery and protection
facts.value: Garage periodically scrubs stored blocks every 25–35 days; it checks block hashes and restores a corrupt block from another valid copy when one exists.

facts.label: file recovery and protection
facts.value: Disconnected nodes are expected to resynchronize when they return; lost-node recovery requires operator action and the documented repair workflow.

facts.label: file recovery and protection
facts.value: There is no built-in object version history or undelete through S3 versioning. Deleting or overwriting an object therefore needs an independent backup to recover prior content.

facts.label: file recovery and protection
facts.value: Garage does not implement S3 Object Lock or legal-hold/retention endpoints.

facts.label: file recovery and protection
facts.value: Garage replication repairs distributed copies but does not replace a separate off-cluster backup. The docs show restic and other S3-compatible backup tools.

facts.label: file recovery and protection
facts.value: Garage does not automatically encrypt stored data at rest under the normal S3 API. Operators can use encrypted disks or SSE-C if their clients support it.

facts.label: identity and old names

facts.label: identity and old names

facts.label: hosting and license

facts.label: hosting and license

facts.value: Deuxfleurs is a French association (association loi 1901) with its registered seat in Lille, France.

facts.label: support and service promises

free.text: 10 GiB Basic/month; subscriptions expire after 31 idle days by default

cells.regions: Global topics; message storage can be region-restricted

Pub/Sub is a messaging service, not a database
