facts.label: Overages and bill controls
facts.value: Hosted budget alerts, invoice caps and quota overage actions do not apply to the GPL software itself.

facts.label: Overages and bill controls
facts.value: Administrators can set database-account limits for queries, updates and connections per hour and simultaneous user connections; these are database resource controls, not monetary spend caps.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: 8.4 max_connections defaults to 151; configurable range 1–100,000. The effective ceiling also depends on open_files_limit and available resources.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: 8.4 server max_allowed_packet defaults to 67,108,864 bytes (64MB in the manual); range 1,024–1,073,741,824 bytes, in 1,024-byte blocks. Client programs can have smaller defaults.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: 8.4 max_execution_time defaults to 0, disabling this timeout. It measures milliseconds for read-only SELECT statements and is ignored for SELECT inside stored programs.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: InnoDB: up to 1,017 columns per table and 64 secondary indexes. Row-size and index-key limits still apply.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: For default 16KB pages, the manual's tablespace-size table gives 64TB; the local filesystem can impose a smaller ceiling. The same page separately describes the internal limit as 64 TiB.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: MySQL's combined column row-size limit is 65,535 bytes; InnoDB's local row portion is slightly less than half a page, with eligible variable-length values stored off-page.

facts.label: File storage prices
facts.value: Not a database-independent object-storage service; no included hot/archive GB-month price.

facts.label: File request and retrieval prices
facts.value: No bundled file-upload/list/retrieval/image-processing request tariff.

facts.label: Minimum storage and early deletion
facts.value: No object-store minimum billed size, retention class or early-deletion schedule to apply.

facts.label: Vector/index limits
facts.value: Current 26.10 VECTOR(N) stores float32 entries: default 2,048 dimensions, maximum 16,383. VECTOR columns cannot be used as primary, foreign, unique or partition keys, or other key types. The documented VECTOR key restriction prevents treating this datatype as an included ANN/vector index. No included Community namespace or billable-index allowance is established by the datatype.

facts.label: Embedding and reranking extras
facts.value: HeatWave on OCI and MySQL AI are separate offerings in these vector docs. Their model/embedding/reranking charges are not an included Community allowance.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: SQL events share the database server's CPU/memory. Community has no per-event invocation, execution-second, retry or waiting-time price, nor a 0.5-vCPU worker SKU.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: Repeating events can overlap if execution takes longer than their interval. The docs recommend explicit locks when overlap must be prevented.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: A public download path offers “No thanks, just start my download.” Oracle account creation is optional on that path; no paid subscription or card is required to obtain the Community download.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: The GPL permits running the program without a production-only or noncommercial-only restriction. Redistribution and modification have their own license conditions.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Oracle website/download access is subject to export and sanctions restrictions; no blanket worldwide eligibility claim is made.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: Primary type: self-hosted relational SQL database. Secondary role: document storage through MySQL Document Store.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Native SQL tables, views, stored procedures/functions, triggers and scheduled SQL events. Database accounts protect database access; application login, upload delivery and general serverless workers need application components.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: MySQL Document Store uses X Protocol and X DevAPI, with MySQL Shell and connectors; relational and document access can coexist.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: Classic MySQL connections support TCP/IP (default port 3306), Unix sockets, and Windows named pipes/shared memory where configured.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: Official connectors include C++, Java/JDBC, .NET, Python, ODBC and Node.js (X Protocol), alongside the C API. Other documented language interfaces can be third-party.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: Database users, host-qualified accounts, grants, roles, account locks and TLS requirements are configurable. A newly created account initially has no privileges and default role NONE.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: With mysqld --initialize, root@localhost gets a generated expired password that must be changed. --initialize-insecure creates it without a password.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: 8.4 require_secure_transport defaults to OFF. Enabling it rejects insecure TCP connections while allowing supported secure local transports.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: Client ssl-mode=PREFERRED attempts encryption but permits fallback. REQUIRED enforces encryption; VERIFY_IDENTITY also verifies the CA and server hostname.

facts.label: Engine and query model
facts.value: MySQL Server uses its own SQL dialect and pluggable storage engines, with InnoDB as the transactional baseline in this record. It is not PostgreSQL or a Postgres-compatible API.

facts.label: Engine and query model
facts.value: Version scope: operational limits and examples use 8.4 LTS; current 26.10 vector features are identified separately.

facts.label: Transactions and consistency
facts.value: InnoDB supports multi-statement START TRANSACTION/COMMIT/ROLLBACK. New connections default to autocommit, so each successful ordinary statement commits on its own unless a transaction is opened.

facts.label: Transactions and consistency
facts.value: InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ; READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED and SERIALIZABLE are also available. Nonlocking reads under REPEATABLE READ share the first read's transaction snapshot.

facts.label: Transactions and consistency
facts.value: Many DDL and account-management statements implicitly commit. A user's ROLLBACK does not undo a normal CREATE TABLE.

facts.label: Test environments and branches
facts.value: Separate development and production instances can run with distinct data directories, ports and socket files. Operators supply and isolate the resources.

facts.label: Test environments and branches
facts.value: Native filesystem snapshots are not supplied by MySQL; snapshot/copy-on-write mechanisms depend on external filesystem solutions. Logical copies are available through dumps.

facts.label: Replicas and failover
facts.value: Source-to-replica replication is asynchronous by default; semisynchronous and deliberately delayed replication are also documented.

facts.label: Replicas and failover
facts.value: Group Replication provides automatic primary election in single-primary mode, but connected clients must be redirected using a connector, load balancer, router or other middleware.

facts.label: Replicas and failover
facts.value: Community includes Group Replication, InnoDB Cluster and Router capabilities; extra database/router machines and their operations remain the operator's responsibility.

facts.label: Live updates and offline sync
facts.value: The binary-log replication interface is a database-to-database change path, not a ready-made browser realtime subscription or offline conflict resolver.

facts.label: Live updates and offline sync
facts.value: A built-in app-client offline-write queue, replay/conflict policy and automatic reconnect synchronization were not established.

facts.label: Extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: FULLTEXT indexes on InnoDB/MyISAM CHAR, VARCHAR and TEXT support natural-language, Boolean and query-expansion searches; ngram and Japanese MeCab parsers are documented.

facts.label: Extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: SPATIAL indexes support NOT NULL geometry columns. Optimizer use requires an explicit SRID restriction so comparisons use the intended spatial reference system.

facts.label: Upload and file limits
facts.value: Multipart/resumable file-upload limits are outside the server's service scope; SQL BLOB transfers instead encounter the database packet and row rules above.

facts.label: S3 and other API compatibility
facts.value: No Community S3 object-service compatibility matrix applies to its MySQL/X Protocol database interface.

facts.label: Delivery and private files
facts.value: Public/private buckets, signed object links, CDN delivery and custom asset domains require a separate delivery layer.

facts.label: Filters and mixed search
facts.value: The 26.10 DISTANCE() function is available only in HeatWave on OCI and MySQL AI, and is explicitly excluded from Community and Commercial distributions.

facts.label: Filters and mixed search
facts.value: Community's documented vector conversion/dimension functions do not establish native dense/sparse hybrid retrieval, ANN filtering or reranking guarantees.

facts.label: Execution model and languages
facts.value: Native scheduled work executes SQL event bodies inside MySQL. The DO body can contain compound SQL; it is not a managed Node.js/Python function runtime or an HTTP delivery queue.

facts.label: Execution model and languages
facts.value: 8.4 event_scheduler defaults to ON; OFF stops event execution, and DISABLED at startup prevents enabling it at runtime.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Events scheduled in the same second have no guaranteed execution order; documented scheduling delay can be 1–2 seconds.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: A managed retry/backoff, deduplication window, dead-letter queue, replay API and exactly-once task guarantee were not found for SQL events.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: One-time AT schedules and recurring EVERY schedules are supported, with optional STARTS/ENDS. Schedule times use the creating session's time zone, stored alongside UTC times. Expired events are dropped by default; ON COMPLETION PRESERVE retains the definition. This is definition retention, not retained execution results.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: INFORMATION_SCHEMA.EVENTS exposes definitions, status and LAST_EXECUTED. LAST_EXECUTED is the latest execution start time, not a complete history of successful completions.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: SELECT/SHOW result sets inside an event are not returned to a client or automatically stored. Persist results explicitly using SQL that writes tables.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: Event execution problems are reported through MySQL's event/error-log monitoring path; the operator manages log handling and retention.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Install a supported MySQL build, initialize a persistent data directory under a suitable OS account, secure database accounts/network access, and operate the server and its storage.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Operators handle upgrades, backup scheduling/retention, restore drills, replicas, monitoring and available capacity. A new Innovation release can require application compatibility work.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Enterprise Backup, Enterprise Audit, Enterprise Firewall and the commercial management/security tool set are separate from the Community entitlement.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Database files are created in an operator-selected data directory. Deployment and backup locations must be chosen and protected by the operator; there is no Community cloud-region selector.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Oracle's services policy covers personal information processed in contracted support/cloud/consulting services; its website policy excludes customers' own collection practices.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: mysqldump exports logical SQL; the mysql client can restore SQL dumps. Delimited-text exports can be loaded using LOAD DATA or mysqlimport.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: DROP DATABASE removes the named database and its tables; database privileges are not automatically removed with it.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: A vendor-managed erasure deadline for an operator's local files is not applicable. Operators must remove exports, replicas, backups and storage snapshots according to their own infrastructure policies.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: Logical backups are available using mysqldump. --single-transaction provides a consistent InnoDB snapshot without blocking normal application changes; concurrent DDL can invalidate or break the dump. Dump coverage must be chosen: --routines and --events include stored routines and event definitions; triggers have their own option. A database dump does not automatically cover server config, external files or infrastructure secrets.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: Point-in-time recovery is possible by restoring a full backup and replaying retained binary-log changes to the desired point.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: Community has no vendor-run backup schedule, retained-day quota or included backup storage. Enterprise Backup is a separate commercial physical-backup product.

facts.label: File recovery and protection
facts.value: Object versions, bucket locks and object undelete are outside this product's file-service scope. Database backups remain applicable under D05.

facts.label: Identity and old names
facts.value: MySQL Community Server; maintained by Oracle. Product URL: https://www.mysql.com/products/community/.

facts.label: Identity and old names
facts.value: Historical ownership: Sun acquired MySQL AB in 2008; Oracle acquired Sun in 2010.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: Community Server 8.4: GPL version 2 only, with the file's additional linking permission for separately licensed included software; software runs on your own infrastructure.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: Oracle also sells commercial licenses; distributing proprietary products with MySQL can require a commercial agreement when GPL distribution requirements are not met.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: Operating and publicly downloadable. The current Community download page presents MySQL Community Server 26.10.0 as a generally available release.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: MySQL 8.0 reached end of life in April 2026 and entered Sustaining Support on April 21, 2026. Oracle recommends 8.4 LTS or 9.7 LTS. Oracle stopped all MySQL Solaris builds and fixes on September 29, 2026, and all builds for RHEL 7, Oracle Linux 7 and CentOS 7 on August 4, 2026.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: Two release tracks: LTS keeps a stable feature set; Innovation permits behavior changes and is supported until the next Innovation release.

facts.label: Vendor home and main markets
facts.value: Oracle Corporation and its affiliates operate globally; the privacy policy says operations in more than 80 countries. This is vendor context, not a MySQL hosting-region list.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: Community support is provided by the open-source developer community; it does not include the paid editions' Premier Support entitlement.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: Commercial subscriptions include Oracle Premier Support: 24×7 support, unlimited support incidents, knowledge base and maintenance releases.

facts.value: NATS Server is separately free-to-use open-source software under Apache-2.0. That is software licensing, not hosted infrastructure or a Synadia Cloud allowance.

facts.label: Cloud plan limits

facts.label: Cloud plan limits
facts.value: The FAQ says additional system safeguards can apply, including subscription and JetStream asset limits. It does not list every such ceiling; Synadia says to ask about increases.

facts.label: Cloud plan limits
facts.value: Synadia Cloud pricing calls replication tiers Standard and HA, while the Cloud management guide says those names are changing to R1 and R3. I keep Standard and HA for the published quotas.

facts.label: Inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: A Personal account lasts while in use, but Synadia reserves the right to delete inactive free accounts. The FAQ does not give an inactivity interval or a guaranteed warning period.

facts.label: Inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: Synadia says free-account storage location may move and free accounts are not guaranteed to meet GDPR requirements.

facts.label: Least paid commitment
facts.value: Synadia Cloud Personal: $0 per month, no card. The plan page does not state an ISO currency code for the dollar symbol.

facts.label: Least paid commitment
facts.value: Synadia Cloud Starter: $49 per month. The public price page shows “$” but does not specify the ISO currency code or tax treatment.

facts.label: Least paid commitment
facts.value: Synadia Cloud Pro: $199 per month. The public price page shows “$” but does not specify the ISO currency code or tax treatment.

facts.label: Least paid commitment
facts.value: Synadia Cloud Enterprise: contact Synadia for a custom price. The public page states that SLA support is available on annual Enterprise contracts.

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Base plans are priced monthly and apply to a Synadia Cloud Team. Personal is free; paid plan base prices are $49/mo and $199/mo for Starter and Pro.

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Remote System add-on, available on all plans: 1 connected NATS system for $49 per month.

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Starter and Pro Connectivity Package: 10 extra connections and 100 extra subscriptions per connection for $10 per month.

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Starter and Pro Leaf Node add-on: 1 extra leaf node for $5 per month.

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Starter and Pro Standard Storage add-on: 1 GiB extra for $0.20 per month.

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Starter and Pro Standard Stream add-on: 1 extra Standard stream and 10 extra Standard consumers per stream for $0.20 per month.

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Starter and Pro HA Storage add-on: 1 GiB extra for $0.90 per month.

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Starter and Pro HA Stream add-on: 1 extra HA stream and 3 extra HA consumers per stream for $5 per month.

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Network overage is measured by traffic type and charged at the end of the monthly billing cycle on paid plans. The page does not name the ISO currency code behind “$”.

facts.label: Idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: Cloud includes a set count of container services and JavaScript functions on Starter and Pro; a separate CPU, memory, idle billing, wake-up, or scale-to-zero rate was not published in the pricing and Workloads pages checked.

facts.label: Idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: Hosted scale-to-zero billing does not apply to the self-hosted NATS Server edition. Operators supply and pay for their own running infrastructure.

facts.label: Data transfer costs
facts.value: Synadia Cloud includes team network data: 10 GiB Personal, 100 GiB Starter, 1 TiB Pro, and 2 TiB Enterprise per pricing table.

facts.label: Data transfer costs
facts.value: Paid-plan client and leaf egress overage: $0.09 per GiB after included network data is exceeded.

facts.label: Data transfer costs
facts.value: Paid-plan gateway egress overage: $0.02 per GiB after included network data is exceeded.

facts.label: Data transfer costs
facts.value: Paid-plan route ingress and egress overage: $0.01 per GiB after included network data is exceeded.

facts.label: Data transfer costs
facts.value: The NATS project publishes no infrastructure transfer tariff for self-hosted use. Network costs depend on the operator’s host or cloud provider and traffic path.

facts.label: Overages and bill controls
facts.value: If Personal network usage exceeds its included allowance, Synadia says active and new client connections will be dropped until the next cycle or an upgrade.

facts.label: Overages and bill controls
facts.value: Paid plans charge published network-data overages at cycle end. Storage, stream, connection, and workload quantities are shown as plan limits and add-ons.

facts.label: Overages and bill controls
facts.value: The pages checked do not state a customer-configurable hard monthly spend cap, exact billing alerts, or what happens when every non-network quota is reached.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: NATS does not publish a generic job execution time, CPU-second meter, or task-run price. Synadia Cloud pricing is based on team plan resources and network data, not an execution charge per message or task run.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: Synadia Cloud workload counts are plan limits, but the public price and workload pages do not publish per-container CPU, RAM, or maximum runtime.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: For JetStream, MaxAckPending defaults to 1,000 unacknowledged messages per consumer; the limit is shared by workers using that consumer and can constrain throughput.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: There is no universal NATS throughput promise. A stream has a leader for writes; throughput can be increased by splitting subjects across streams and adding workers, while replication improves resilience rather than write throughput.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: A Synadia Cloud capacity or throughput figure beyond the plan table was not published in the pricing, FAQ, or workload pages checked.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Synadia Cloud offers self-service Personal access at $0 per month without a credit card. No signup form was submitted.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Synadia describes Personal as for individual developers and hobbyists. Because Cloud-specific customer terms were not located, the checked pages do not establish whether production use is allowed.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: A full list of eligible signup countries or geographic account restrictions was not published in the Cloud pricing, FAQ, and service overview pages checked.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: Primary directory type: jobs, queues, and events. NATS routes messages by subject; JetStream adds durable streams, replay, and consumer state.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: NATS also supports request/reply, pub/sub, key-value and object storage, MQTT and WebSocket connections, and service discovery. It is a messaging/data layer, not a hosted relational database or a general function runner.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Core NATS provides pub/sub, request/reply, and queue-group messaging. Core messages are transient and are delivered only to subscribers connected when the message is published.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: JetStream adds persistent streams, durable consumer state, message replay, key-value buckets, and object stores. Cloud pricing includes a pooled allowance for Standard and HA JetStream storage.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Synadia Cloud adds a managed control plane to create accounts and users, manage streams and consumers, review usage, and configure imports, exports, and alerts.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Cloud plans can include hosted container services, TypeScript/JavaScript functions, and connectors. The plan table limits their counts; it does not publish the CPU or memory size of those workloads.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: NATS has official Tier 1 client libraries for Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Java, Rust, C#/.NET, and C. Java can also be used from Kotlin and Scala.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: The native NATS client port defaults to 4222. The official quick start exposes 8222 for optional HTTP monitoring; it does not mean monitoring should be exposed publicly.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: NATS supports TLS connections and a WebSocket transport. Synadia Cloud offers a geo-balanced default endpoint and regional TLS endpoints; regional endpoints also support WebSocket clients.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: Synadia Cloud has a REST control-plane API as well as the NATS messaging protocol. Apps use standard NATS client SDKs and the Cloud credentials file.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: NATS supports per-user publish/subscribe permissions scoped to subjects and account-level separation; accounts can set connection and JetStream storage limits.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: TLS is configured separately for client, cluster, leaf-node, gateway, and monitoring links. Self-host operators must configure each connection type they expose.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: JetStream disk encryption is available as a server-wide configured option; it is not enabled merely by turning on JetStream. TLS alone protects data in transit, not stored data.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: Synadia says Cloud account and user keys are encrypted with 256-bit encryption; root account keys do not leave the application.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: Synadia’s security page says data is encrypted in transit and JetStream disks use provider disk encryption, but unencrypted data can be in memory and system operators with VM root access could theoretically access it.

facts.label: Execution model and languages
facts.value: NATS is a broker that routes client messages. It does not execute ordinary application jobs for self-hosters; workers run in applications that connect to NATS. Synadia Cloud can separately host plan-limited container workloads and JavaScript functions.

facts.label: Execution model and languages
facts.value: Official client SDKs cover Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Java, Rust, C#/.NET, and C. The Cloud Workloads page documents container workloads and JavaScript functions in a Deno isolate.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Core NATS is at-most-once and transient: a disconnected subscriber does not get a message later.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: JetStream consumers track acknowledgments. If an acknowledged-delivery message is not acked before its configured wait, JetStream redelivers it; applications should make side effects safe against repeats.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: A pull consumer lets workers request a bounded batch or continuous consumption; multiple workers can share one consumer and divide its messages.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: JetStream has configurable Limits, Interest, and WorkQueue retention policies. WorkQueue removes a message after a worker acknowledges it; it is not the same guarantee as exactly-once application side effects.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: A JetStream stream can be capped by message count, bytes, age, or per-subject count. The user chooses limits; there is no single fixed retention duration for all streams.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Streams use file or memory storage. File storage survives a server restart; memory storage does not. Configure file storage and a store directory for durable messages.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: The server default client max_payload is 1 MB. It is configurable up to 64 MB, though NATS advises against values above 8 MB; max_payload cannot exceed max_pending.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: NATS Server 2.15 sets a default limit of 1,000 consumers per stream when no explicit limit is set; operators can configure another default or unlimited.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Synadia Cloud maximum message size is 1 MiB Personal, 1 MiB Starter, 2 MiB Pro, and 8 MiB Enterprise. Cloud includes message-size limits in its plan; these differ from the self-host server’s configurable maximum.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: JetStream stores stream messages and consumer position for replay; how long messages remain depends on the configured retention and size limits.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: Synadia Cloud’s plan table sets storage and stream counts, not a fixed log-history period. The customer’s stream age/size settings determine message retention within the account allowance.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: Snapshots and restore are available for self-managed JetStream file streams. Replication is not a backup, and memory streams cannot be snapshotted by the documented procedure.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The server is a single binary and is available in the official Docker image. The getting-started example maps client port 4222 and optional monitoring port 8222.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: JetStream is opt-in on the server. Start it with the -js flag or enable it in server configuration; choose a persistent store directory for file-backed data.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: A single server with one stream replica is not fault tolerant. Three replicas across three servers can tolerate one server loss; five replicas are the documented maximum and tolerate two server losses.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: File storage survives a server restart; memory storage is lost on restart. Replicated streams require a cluster and a quorum; more replicas do not increase write throughput.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The server configuration reference lists default maximum client connections of 64K, default maximum payload of 1 MB, and default per-client max_pending of 64 MB. These are configurable server limits, not throughput targets.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: NATS describes the server as a small binary but does not publish a universal minimum CPU, RAM, disk, or monthly infrastructure budget. Actual needs depend on message rates, payload size, retention, replicas, and consumers.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The operator is responsible for server deployment, configuration, upgrades, monitoring, data backups, key protection, and restoring streams. NATS supplies official backup and upgrade guides.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Monitoring endpoints can expose server, connection, route, and JetStream details; enable and protect them as part of the deployment.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: NATS Server licensing is Apache-2.0, while hosting, disks, bandwidth, and operations remain the self-hoster’s costs. No paid NATS Server license is required for commercial use under the published license.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Synadia Cloud’s hosted team usage limits, invoices, storage add-ons, and network overages do not apply to self-hosted NATS Server.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: NATS Server’s default network listener is not encrypted unless TLS is configured. Client, cluster, leaf-node, gateway, and monitoring connections have separate TLS settings.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: The Cloud product page lists four named service locations: ap-east-2 (Taipei), aws-euwest-1 (Dublin), aws-useast-2 (Ohio), and aws-uswest-2 (Oregon).

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Regional connection endpoints are available for Asia-Pacific, Europe, U.S., Western U.S., and Eastern U.S. The default connect.ngs.global endpoint is geo-balanced to a nearby server.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Cloud JetStream streams, key-value buckets, and object stores can use placement tags for U.S., Western U.S., Eastern U.S., Europe, or Asia-Pacific. The default placement is near the client and may also depend on resource balance and plan.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Synadia says a resource that cannot satisfy its placement tags can fail with an insufficient-resources error. The tags are placement controls, not a legal-compliance certification.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Self-hosted NATS stores data on the operator-selected hosts and disks. NATS does not choose a hosted region for the self-hosted server.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: NATS CLI supports stream backup and restore. Operators can separately back up server configuration and account identity files; those are needed alongside message data for recovery.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Three JetStream replicas provide availability, not backup: an accidental delete or corrupt write is also applied to every replica. Keep a separate snapshot for rollback.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Synadia Cloud lets a Team owner delete a Team and its associated resources; a user can delete their account, removing personal data and Personal Teams they created.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Cloud documentation checked does not specify the delay before associated data is physically removed or a self-service bulk export for all Cloud configuration and activity.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: NATS Server itself does not control removal of self-hosted data. The operator controls the files and backups in its configured store directory.

facts.label: Identity and old names
facts.value: NATS is an open-source messaging system. The requested product is the NATS Server with its JetStream persistence layer; NATS is also the name of the CNCF project.

facts.label: Identity and old names
facts.value: Synadia Cloud is Synadia’s managed hosted NATS service and the main hosted option checked for this record. NGS is the name used in older Cloud docs for the global NATS service behind it.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: NATS Server is self-hosted software available as a single server binary. JetStream, clustering, leaf nodes, MQTT, and WebSocket are configured on that server.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: The current NATS Server license is Apache License 2.0. The server license file does not impose a use fee.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: Synadia Cloud is a managed SaaS service built on NATS; users connect with NATS client SDKs and Synadia operates its infrastructure. Its hosted service terms are separate from the Apache license for the NATS Server code.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: A Cloud-specific public customer Terms of Service and Privacy Policy were not located in Synadia Cloud pricing, docs, and the Synadia site pages checked. The available Synadia Deploy enterprise terms concern a different offer and were not applied to Synadia Cloud.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: NATS is active. The CNCF project profile records its move from Incubating to Graduated on November 2, 2026.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: The latest stable server release is v2.15.2, released October 26, 2026.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: NATS 2.15 is the latest supported release line; 2.14 is also maintained. NATS docs mark 2.12 and 2.11 end of life.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: In the May 2025 resolution, Synadia agreed to assign its NATS trademark registrations to the Linux Foundation; CNCF retained project infrastructure including nats.io and the GitHub repositories. NATS development remains under Apache-2.0.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: Synadia’s follow-up says NATS remains a CNCF Apache-2.0 project, that Synadia will continue investing in and maintaining NATS, and that it decided not to fork NATS Server under BSL.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: CNCF’s June 2025 board minutes characterize the dispute as positively resolved with strengthened CNCF-Synadia collaboration.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: No acquisition, shutdown, or retirement notice was found in the NATS blog, Synadia blog/newsletter, CNCF project/news pages, project releases, or the joint resolution statement.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: The 2.15 release blog highlights reliability, stream backup/restore improvements, and safer scaling and movement of streams and consumers. It is a recent release, not a notice that all older versions are supported.

facts.label: Vendor home and main markets
facts.value: A current Synadia business headquarters or country was not stated on the official About, Cloud, pricing, or FAQ pages checked. Cloud is described as global and multi-cloud; that does not identify the company’s home country.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: NATS Server users can report bugs and request help through the public GitHub repository and NATS community channels; this is community support, not a vendor uptime promise.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: Synadia Cloud customers may report service issues by email. The pricing page says Synadia troubleshoots customer NATS applications only under an Enterprise support contract.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: Synadia Cloud support portal access and a chosen response-time SLA are included with annual Enterprise contracts. Starter and Pro list no support SLA.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: A public Synadia Cloud uptime percentage or status-page address was not found in the pricing page, FAQ, overview, or security page checked.

facts.label: engine and query model

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: Neo4j transactions provide atomic commit/rollback and durability; default isolation is read committed, not serializable. Concurrent updates can cause non-repeatable reads/lost-update patterns unless query dependencies or explicit locks protect them.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: Cluster/secondary readers can use bookmarks for causal consistency and read-your-writes. Enterprise primaries synchronously confirm a write quorum; secondaries are asynchronously replicated.

facts.label: replicas and failover

facts.label: Data access controls

facts.label: Transactions and consistency
facts.value: Default isolation level, read-after-write guarantees across components and transactional behavior of cross-database/remote operations not specified in the searched Nhost pages.

facts.label: Upload and file limits
facts.value: Numeric global/plan maximum file size and resumable/S3-style multipart part limits not established.

facts.value: Native SQL/pgvector offers L2, inner-product and cosine similarity; pg_search adds BM25 keyword search. Auto-embeddings queries expose maxDistance filtering; normal GraphQL permissions apply to exposed data.

facts.value: Managed HTTP functions execute JavaScript/TypeScript on Node.js 22, 24 (default) or 26; Express-style request/response. Bundling supports JS dependencies, not native add-ons. Use Run for arbitrary Docker/container runtimes.

facts.label: Execution model and languages
facts.value: Hasura events coordinate HTTP deliveries for database changes, cron and one-off schedules; handlers may be Nhost Functions, Run or external services. pg_durable separately provides SQL durable workflows inside Postgres.

facts.value: Hasura HTTP delivery retries on non-2xx/network errors when configured. Defaults: numRetries=0, intervalSeconds=10, timeoutSeconds=60; scheduled-event toleranceSeconds=21600. Configured attempts can redeliver effects.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Database event dashboard supports per-invocation logs and manual Redeliver. Native exactly-once side effects, ordering, deduplication window and dead-letter-queue policy not established.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Maximum future delay, pending-event retention/TTL, payload ceiling and expired/failed message retention not found.

facts.value: Hosted log/event-history retained days/bytes by plan, export facility and additional retention/export fees not found.

facts.label: Free offer type
facts.value: OpenSearch is free, self-hosted software under Apache 2.0; it is not a hosted free tier or trial.

facts.label: Free limits
facts.value: Not applicable as a hosted free-plan allowance: this record covers self-hosted software without an OpenSearch-project account quota. Engine limits are recorded under D03 and V01.

facts.label: Inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: Not applicable to vendor-managed sleep, expiry, or deletion: the operator runs the cluster and controls its processes, disks, snapshots, and retention.

facts.label: Least paid commitment
facts.value: OpenSearch has no software subscription commitment under Apache 2.0. The minimum infrastructure bill depends on the operator's chosen hosts, storage, and backup service.

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Not applicable to project software billing: the self-hosted project does not meter documents, queries, storage, or compute for a vendor invoice. Provider and model bills remain separate.

facts.label: Idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: Not applicable to hosted product-level scale-to-zero billing. A self-hosted cluster uses the operator's machines while running; stopping nodes and any continuing storage charges depend on the operator's setup.

facts.label: Data transfer costs
facts.value: Not applicable to a project egress tariff. Network and object-storage transfer charges, if any, are set by the operator's infrastructure providers.

facts.label: Overages and bill controls
facts.value: Not applicable to project-level overages or spend caps because the source project does not issue a metered service bill. Provider budget tools do not belong to OpenSearch itself.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: A knn_vector field dimension is limited to 1 through 16,000. The field supports float, half-float, byte, and binary values in the current docs.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: A k-NN query can request k from 1 through 10,000 results.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: The default maximum of from + size for ordinary search pagination is 10,000 per index; the setting can be changed, but deep pagination costs more resources.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: The default maximum mapped field count is 1,000 per index. The setting is configurable; the docs warn that large mappings increase memory and can hurt performance.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: The default maximum HTTP request body is 100 MB, controlled by the static http.max_content_length setting. This applies to request content, including a bulk body, not to a separate universal single-document size limit.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: Default cluster shard limit is 1,000 primary plus replica shards per non-frozen data node; it is configurable. Default primary shards per new index is 1 and replicas default to 1.

facts.label: Capacity and connection limits
facts.value: A fixed maximum document count, active-client connection count, or per-document byte maximum for all self-hosted deployments was not found in the limits, networking, or index-setting docs checked.

facts.label: Storage prices
facts.value: Not applicable: OpenSearch is a search/index engine, not a general-purpose user file or object storage service.

facts.label: File request and retrieval prices
facts.value: Not applicable: OpenSearch does not sell end-user file upload, download, listing, or object-retrieval operations.

facts.label: Minimum storage and early deletion
facts.value: Not applicable: OpenSearch has no user-facing hot/archive file tiers or file-retention tariff.

facts.label: Vector/index limits
facts.value: The documented knn_vector dimension range is 1 to 16,000. Current data types include float, half-float, byte, and binary; v3.9 adds native half-float and new quantization options.

facts.label: Vector/index limits
facts.value: k-NN k is limited to 10,000 per query. There is no universal vector count ceiling in the vector field docs; usable data depends on storage, memory, index method, and shard layout.

facts.label: Vector/index limits
facts.value: Approximate k-NN engines and methods include Lucene HNSW and Faiss methods such as HNSW and IVF; JVector is supplied by its project plugin. NMSLIB appears as deprecated in current filter docs.

facts.label: Vector/index limits
facts.value: k-NN native-memory use has a configurable circuit breaker. Its default limit is 50% of memory remaining after JVM allocation, rather than a fixed storage quota.

facts.label: Embedding and reranking extras
facts.value: OpenSearch can run some local models through ML Commons and can connect to remote providers including OpenAI, Cohere, Amazon SageMaker, Amazon Bedrock, and Google Vertex AI.

facts.label: Embedding and reranking extras
facts.value: Provider inference charges, model availability, and rate limits belong to the external model service; OpenSearch does not set one common token price.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: Not applicable to user-code invocation pricing. OpenSearch does not meter application functions or worker execution time.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Self-hosted binaries, containers, and source are publicly available from the project without a project account or signup.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Apache 2.0 permits commercial production use under its conditions. Commercial use of the OpenSearch name must also follow the project trademark policy and must not imply project endorsement.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: The OpenSearch community forum's Terms of Service apply to forum use and say other products may have different terms. The forum privacy page links to the Linux Foundation privacy policy; neither is a policy for a self-hosted cluster.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: Primary type: self-hosted document search and analytics engine, with vector search as a built-in use case through the k-NN and Neural Search plugins. It indexes JSON documents and fields rather than relational rows.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: The self-hosted distribution provides document indexing, full-text and structured search, aggregations, vector search, and REST APIs. It is a search/data engine, not a complete app backend with end-user accounts, file buckets, or general application hosting.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: OpenSearch Dashboards is the project's browser-based interface for exploring data and managing queries; it is separately released and installed.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Search features include BM25 text search, SQL/PPL query plugins, geospatial fields, k-NN vector retrieval, hybrid search, and optional machine-learning integrations.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: OpenSearch can generate embeddings with configured local models or connect to external inference providers, but those model services and their charges are separate.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: REST covers every documented operation. The detailed gRPC API page marks Bulk and k-NN as generally available since 3.2, while other gRPC search functions remain experimental; the general API reference still broadly calls the gRPC subset experimental.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: Official clients are listed for Python, Java, JavaScript for Node.js, Go, Ruby, PHP, .NET, and Rust, plus a Hadoop connector.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: The client list and connection docs do not give a universal guarantee for browser-native, edge, or every serverless runtime.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: The Security plugin supports internal users and roles, external authentication backends, and index-level permissions. OpenSearch also supports document-level and field-level security when configured.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: Setup quickstarts use a demo security configuration with self-signed certificates and published demo-user passwords. Production setup requires replacing demo certificates and credentials.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: OpenSearch supports TLS on REST and transport connections; the operator supplies trusted production certificates and configures the network boundary.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: External identity integrations include LDAP, SAML, and OpenID Connect, in addition to the Security plugin's internal user database.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: OpenSearch does not provide a hosted application's end-user signup, session, or user-management service. Its security plugin controls access to the search cluster and indexed documents.

facts.label: Engine and query model
facts.value: OpenSearch stores JSON documents in indexes with mapped fields, then searches them through Query DSL and REST endpoints. It is document-oriented and does not implement the relational-table model of PostgreSQL or MySQL.

facts.label: Engine and query model
facts.value: The SQL plugin accepts SQL and PPL queries and translates them to OpenSearch operations; SQL support is a query interface over document indexes, not evidence of relational storage or full relational transaction semantics.

facts.label: Transactions and consistency
facts.value: Writes use document-level versioning and optimistic concurrency controls. By default, a successful write becomes searchable after refresh, typically within about one second; refresh can be forced or awaited.

facts.label: Transactions and consistency
facts.value: I did not find a multi-document ACID transaction or rollback contract. Bulk requests contain multiple document operations, but the docs describe per-document concurrency and refresh behavior.

facts.label: Test environments and branches
facts.value: Index aliases, separate indexes, and separate clusters can support blue/green release and test workflows.

facts.label: Test environments and branches
facts.value: I did not find a native copy-on-write branch feature for cloning a live database/index. The docs cover aliases, reindexing, snapshots, and separate clusters instead.

facts.label: Replicas and failover
facts.value: Index replicas copy primary shard data across nodes; default replica count for a newly created index is 1 unless changed at index or cluster level.

facts.label: Replicas and failover
facts.value: Cross-cluster replication sends changes from a leader index to one or more read-only follower indexes. The operator configures both clusters, permissions, and remote connections.

facts.label: Replicas and failover
facts.value: A universal RTO/RPO or automatic client failover guarantee is not part of the self-hosted software docs checked. Operators must design failover and point clients to a healthy cluster.

facts.label: Live updates and offline sync
facts.value: OpenSearch refresh controls when indexed documents become searchable, but it is not a browser/mobile offline database or a client-side changefeed service.

facts.label: Live updates and offline sync
facts.value: Durable offline writes, bidirectional sync, client subscriptions, and conflict resolution were not found in REST API, client, replication, or search documentation.

facts.label: Extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: OpenSearch supports BM25 full-text search, geo_point and geo_shape fields, and vector search through k-NN/Neural Search. SQL/PPL are available through their query plugin.

facts.label: Extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: The k-NN plugin supports Lucene and Faiss engines; the separate JVector plugin adds a JVector engine. Engine, algorithm, filtering, and compression combinations differ.

facts.label: Upload and file limits
facts.value: Not applicable to end-user file uploads. The 100 MB HTTP request-body default is a database request limit recorded under D03, not a user-file product limit.

facts.label: S3 and other API compatibility
facts.value: Not applicable as a user-facing object-storage API: OpenSearch does not expose an S3-compatible user bucket. It can write internal snapshots to configured repository types.

facts.label: Delivery and private files
facts.value: Not applicable: there are no app file buckets, signed download links, CDN, or file-serving domains in the self-hosted search engine.

facts.label: Filters and mixed search
facts.value: k-NN queries support filters, but efficient in-search filtering varies by engine and method. Hybrid queries combine lexical and vector queries; hybrid search supports pre- and post-filtering.

facts.label: Filters and mixed search
facts.value: Multi-tenant search can use mapped tenant fields and filters plus Security plugin index, document, and field-level access rules. A filter alone is not authorization.

facts.label: Execution model and languages
facts.value: Not applicable as a general-purpose application worker: OpenSearch indexes and searches data. ML inference and plugin tasks are database features, not a customer code runtime.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Not applicable as a general application queue: OpenSearch does not expose a customer queue with delivery, retry, and deduplication semantics.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Not applicable as a customer task scheduler or queue-retention service. Snapshot Management and other plugins schedule database maintenance tasks only.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: Not applicable to hosted application run-history or customer worker-log retention. Self-hosted operators decide how long server logs and metrics remain.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Supported installation methods include Docker, Helm, Kubernetes Operator, tarball, RPM, Debian packages, Ansible, and Windows installation.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The 3.9 operating-system test matrix lists Rocky Linux 8, AlmaLinux 8, Amazon Linux 2023, Ubuntu 24.04, and Windows Server 2019.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The 3.9 distribution bundles Java 25.0.4.1+1 and supports Java 21, 25, and 26.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The installation guide recommends SSDs for node storage and warns against network filesystems for production node storage because latency and throughput can hurt performance.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: A universal RAM/CPU minimum or safe node size for a production search workload was not found in the installation and cluster-tuning pages checked.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Production self-hosting requires replacing demo credentials and certificates, configuring roles and network access, sizing a multi-node topology, and scheduling and testing snapshots.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Self-hosted OpenSearch has no project region selector. The operator chooses where the cluster nodes and local disks run.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Snapshot locations are also operator-selected: current docs describe local/shared filesystems, Amazon S3, HDFS, and Azure Storage repositories. Their region and residency behavior comes from the chosen storage provider.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Snapshots can copy index data and selected cluster state to a registered repository. Supported repository types include shared filesystem, Amazon S3, HDFS, and Azure Storage.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Snapshots are incremental and not an exact point-in-time view of concurrent writes: each shard reflects its state when that shard's snapshot starts. Use the Snapshot Management plugin to schedule snapshots and delete old ones by policy.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Snapshots restore to the same or a newer compatible cluster, not an older version. They are forward-compatible by one major version; older-version migration can require intermediate upgrades and reindexing.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: The operator deletes indexes or the cluster and separately deletes snapshots and provider storage. I did not find a project-level account-deletion or guaranteed secure-erasure clock for self-hosted data.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: Snapshot repositories support shared filesystem, Amazon S3, HDFS, and Azure Storage. Snapshots can include indexes and selected cluster metadata.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: The Snapshot Management plugin can schedule incremental snapshots and delete old snapshots by policy; no snapshot cadence is configured automatically for a new self-hosted installation.

facts.label: Backups and restore
facts.value: Snapshot restore is forward-compatible by one major version and does not support restoring to an older version. An older snapshot may need intermediate restores and reindexing.

facts.label: File recovery and protection
facts.value: Not applicable to user-file versioning or object lock. OpenSearch snapshots back up search indexes and selected cluster state instead.

facts.label: Identity and former names
facts.value: OpenSearch is the open-source search and analytics project at opensearch.org. It began as a fork of Elasticsearch 7.10.2 and Kibana 7.10.2; it is a separate project, not the current Elasticsearch product under another name.

facts.label: Identity and former names
facts.value: The OpenSearch Software Foundation, a project of the Linux Foundation, supports the project.

facts.value: Self-hosted OpenSearch and OpenSearch Dashboards are available as open-source distributions. The project FAQ states that all software in the OpenSearch project uses Apache License 2.0.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: The Apache 2.0 license allows commercial use, modification, and redistribution subject to the license conditions.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: Amazon OpenSearch Service is a separate AWS-managed product. AWS offers managed domains and OpenSearch Serverless collections under AWS service terms, account controls, regional availability, and billing.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: Aiven for OpenSearch is another separate managed product; the OpenSearch project lists it as a solutions provider.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: The OpenSearch trademark policy governs how the project name and logos may be used in branding and service descriptions.

facts.value: Active. The latest OpenSearch engine release checked is 3.9.0, released September 29, 2026. The latest OpenSearch Dashboards release checked is also 3.9.0, released October 12, 2026.

facts.label: Free limits
facts.value: For paid accounts or accounts with active Free Trial credits, Oracle lists 10 GB Standard, 10 GB Infrequent Access, 10 GB Archive, and 50,000 Object Storage API requests per month as Always Free resources.

facts.label: Free limits
facts.value: The public global price list also labels the first 10 GB/month of Standard, Infrequent Access, and Archive storage as Free Tier.

facts.label: Free limits

facts.label: Free limits

facts.label: Free limits

facts.label: Least paid commitment
facts.value: The smallest ongoing Object Storage commitment is no fixed monthly fee when there is no billable overage; actual spend starts when usage exceeds free allowances.

facts.label: Least paid commitment
facts.value: The standard US Cloud Services Agreement says listed fees exclude applicable taxes and expenses; the customer is responsible for sales, value-added, or similar taxes.

facts.label: Billing meters

facts.label: Billing meters
facts.value: Object Storage usage from versioning, lifecycle management, replication, pending multipart uploads, SDKs, and third-party tools can create billable storage or API usage.

facts.label: Data transfer costs

facts.label: Data transfer costs

facts.label: Data transfer costs

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: The Free Trial offers USD $300 in credits for up to 30 days; credits expire when used or at the 30-day limit.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Oracle's Free Tier signup instructions say one OCI cloud account can be created per email address.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Oracle says most users need a mobile phone number and credit card to create an account; the card is not charged unless the account is upgraded.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Oracle's Free Tier is offered in regions where commercial OCI is available; if a country or territory is not listed, Oracle directs applicants to Sales or Cloud Support.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: The standard US Cloud Services Agreement limits use to the customer's internal business operations and bars making the Services available to third parties or commercially exploiting them except as permitted by the order; the public product FAQ does not clarify every app-end-user use case.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: Primary role is managed regional object storage for unstructured data and files.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: Secondary uses include backup destinations, static assets, analytics data, archive, and Hadoop/Spark input; these are use cases, not separate application-backend services.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Object Storage includes buckets, objects, upload/download/list/delete APIs, and Standard, Infrequent Access, and Archive storage tiers.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Bucket features include lifecycle rules, versioning, retention rules, replication, object events, encryption, and access policies.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Object Storage can serve static files, but it does not execute application code; Oracle's docs do not describe a bundled application server in this product.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: HDFS connector support lets Hadoop and Spark jobs read and write Object Storage data; the connector is a separate client integration, not a managed compute runtime in Object Storage.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Optional Auto-Tiering monitors access patterns and moves eligible objects larger than 1 MiB between Standard and Infrequent Access; frequently accessed objects can move back without IA retrieval or early-deletion charges.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: The native OCI Object Storage API is a regional HTTPS API; the endpoint includes the OCI region identifier.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: Official OCI SDKs are available for Java, Python, TypeScript/JavaScript, .NET, Go, Ruby, and PL/SQL; an OCI CLI is also available.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: The service supports an Amazon S3 Compatibility API and OpenStack Swift API in addition to the native OCI API.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: Oracle's HDFS connector supports Hadoop 2.7.2 and can connect Hadoop/Spark workloads to Object Storage.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: The S3 Compatibility API supports path-style and virtual-hosted-style URLs, but AWS Signature Version 2 is unsupported; a client must send a supported signature and OCI region endpoint.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: New buckets are private by default and require authenticated, authorized access; Oracle says data travels over HTTPS and is encrypted at rest by default.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: OCI IAM policies can grant bucket and object permissions; Object Storage supports object-level access control as well as compartment- and bucket-level controls.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: A pre-authenticated request can grant scoped read, write, or read/write access to a bucket, object, or prefix without sharing the requester's account credentials.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: A pre-authenticated request requires an expiry time; Oracle allows any future expiry and does not let an existing request be edited.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: Private access can use a VCN service gateway or Object Storage private endpoint; policies can restrict access by VCN or CIDR.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: Customer-managed Vault keys and customer-provided encryption keys are optional; Oracle-managed at-rest encryption is enabled by default.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: Oracle's Services Privacy Policy treats the customer as controller of Services Personal Information and Oracle as processor acting on the customer's documented instructions; the applicable order/DPA takes precedence if privacy terms conflict.

facts.label: Upload and file limits
facts.value: Oracle documents unlimited total object storage and unlimited objects per bucket, with a service limit of 10,000 buckets per tenancy.

facts.label: Upload and file limits
facts.value: Maximum object size is 10 TiB; a single PutObject request is limited to 50 GiB.

facts.label: Upload and file limits
facts.value: Multipart upload supports up to 10,000 parts, each up to 50 GiB.

facts.label: Upload and file limits
facts.value: Oracle recommends multipart uploads for objects larger than 100 MiB.

facts.label: Upload and file limits
facts.value: Object metadata assigned to one object is limited to 4,000 bytes total.

facts.label: Upload and file limits
facts.value: User-specified bucket names are 1–256 characters, case-sensitive, unique within the namespace, and may use letters, digits, hyphens, underscores, and periods.

facts.label: Upload and file limits
facts.value: Oracle does not publish a general file-type allowlist for Object Storage objects; it stores objects of any content type.

facts.value: The native Object Storage API is Oracle's primary API; Oracle also offers an S3 Compatibility API and Swift API.

facts.value: S3 Compatibility API requires an OCI region endpoint and OCI Customer Secret Key; AWS Signature Version 2 is not supported.

facts.value: S3-compatible client use is not identical to AWS S3: OCI uses namespaces and compartments, and supports its own documented operation set and endpoint rules.

facts.label: S3 and other API compatibility
facts.value: Oracle provides a Hadoop HDFS connector for reading and writing Object Storage data; this is a connector, not an NFS or SMB mount.

facts.label: S3 and other API compatibility
facts.value: Oracle's FAQ says Object Storage buckets cannot be mounted as traditional NFS/SMB paths; access is through APIs, SDKs, CLI, or HDFS connector.

facts.label: Delivery and private files
facts.value: Buckets are private by default; access requires authentication and authorization unless anonymous public access is deliberately enabled.

facts.label: Delivery and private files
facts.value: Pre-authenticated requests provide expiring read/write access to a bucket, object, or prefix without sharing user credentials.

facts.label: Delivery and private files
facts.value: OCI Object Storage APIs return CORS headers, but Oracle says the returned CORS headers are fixed and cannot be edited.

facts.label: Delivery and private files
facts.value: The product FAQ and Object Storage docs checked do not publish a built-in CDN, custom-domain, or CDN pricing feature for this service.

facts.label: Delivery and private files
facts.value: Public object access and private pre-authenticated URLs are both supported; the latter can restrict access by object/prefix and expiry.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Oracle lists Object Storage availability across its public cloud regions; availability is still region-specific and the live status page distinguishes regions where a service is not offered.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Object Storage can replicate objects to a destination bucket in the same region or a different OCI region; this is optional replication, not automatic cross-region residency.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Oracle's current DPA says cloud personal information is stored in the region specified in the order or selected for the production service, while Oracle may access it globally as needed to perform the service.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Always Free resources are offered in the tenancy's home region; Oracle's free-tier page excludes US Government Cloud regions.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Oracle's hosting and delivery policy provides up to 60 days after production service termination or expiry to retrieve customer data using secure protocols; Oracle has no retention duty after that period.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: For free trials, Oracle's hosting policy provides a 30-day retrieval window after trial termination; the service SLA does not apply during that window.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Without versioning, deleting or overwriting an object is not recoverable through Object Storage; bucket versioning can retain prior versions until explicitly removed.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Oracle's Services Privacy Policy says that after service termination it will return or delete remaining production customer data, except where the order or law says otherwise; the hosting policy separately gives the production retrieval window.

facts.label: File recovery and protection
facts.value: Versioning can retain prior object versions after overwrite or delete; prior versions remain billable until explicitly deleted.

facts.label: File recovery and protection
facts.value: Lifecycle policies can move or delete objects and versions, including cleanup of incomplete multipart uploads; policies support up to 1,000 rules per bucket.

facts.label: File recovery and protection
facts.value: Lifecycle rules normally run within 10 minutes on a best-effort basis and can take 24 hours or longer for very large buckets; billing remains at the existing tier until processing completes.

facts.label: File recovery and protection
facts.value: Retention rules can prevent update, overwrite, or delete for a time-bound period or indefinitely; a locked rule can be removed only by deleting its empty bucket.

facts.label: File recovery and protection
facts.value: Replication asynchronously copies new objects to a same-region or cross-region destination bucket; source deletions are also propagated, and pre-policy objects are not copied.

facts.label: File recovery and protection
facts.value: Data is redundantly stored across multiple availability domains within a region and checksum-checked; versioning and retention rules are optional controls for recovery from user changes.

facts.label: Identity and old names

facts.label: Identity and old names

facts.label: Hosting and license

facts.value: No Object Storage shutdown, sunset, or acquisition notice was located in the product release notes, OCI blog, Oracle News/press newsroom, or Oracle Investor News checked.

facts.value: Oracle says technical support for production OCI workloads is included in base service fees, with no separate support fee.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: Oracle's Free Tier FAQ says Free Tier does not include an SLA and points users to community forums for support.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: The Object Storage tier table lists 99.9% availability SLA for Standard and 99% for Infrequent Access; Archive objects are offline until restored and the tier table gives no percentage SLA for Archive access.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: Oracle's formal OCI SLA includes Object Storage for control-plane service-level coverage; this should not be read as a separate data-plane uptime promise for every tier.

facts.value: Oracle provides a public OCI status dashboard with regional service state and incident history.
