facts.label: free offer type
facts.value: Free software with commercial production permission; not a hosted free tier, expiring trial or cloud credit. Software license fee is zero, while servers, storage, backups and operations remain the user's responsibility.

facts.label: free limits
facts.value: Vendor-hosted free GB, compute, read/write, MAU, project and seat allowances are not applicable. Software capacity limits are documented separately under D03.

facts.label: inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: Vendor inactivity pause/deletion timers and restore grace periods are not applicable to the self-hosted distribution. The operator controls shutdown and retained files.

facts.label: least paid commitment
facts.value: A least paid hosted plan, subscription/seat commitment and hosted tax price are not applicable.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Vendor billing meters, usage rounding, failed-request fees and paid plan add-ons are not applicable to PostgreSQL software.

facts.label: idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: Managed compute scale-to-zero billing and automatic wake policies are not applicable. An operator can stop/start the database; that alone does not define whether an external server or disk stops charging.

facts.label: data transfer costs
facts.value: Vendor ingress/egress/inter-region tariffs and free transfer allowances are not applicable. Costs depend on the operator's network/storage provider.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: Vendor usage overages, monetary spend caps and billing alerts are not applicable to the software distribution.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: PG18 hard limits include 32 TB per relation at default 8,192-byte blocks, 1 GB per field, up to 1,600 table columns (also page-size constrained), and 65,535 query parameters. Database size is listed as unlimited, subject to practical storage/performance limits.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: max_connections is typically 100, possibly lower after initdb kernel checks; it is startup-configurable and consumes more shared resources when raised. Three slots default to superuser reserve; additional reserved_connections defaults zero.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: Core statement_timeout and transaction_timeout default to zero, meaning disabled; operators can set them. These are execution/session controls, not subscription quotas or a promise any query can finish with finite resources.

facts.label: storage prices
facts.value: Hosted object/file storage class tariffs do not apply.

facts.label: file request and retrieval prices
facts.value: Upload/list/retrieval/image-processing per-request prices are not applicable.

facts.label: minimum storage and early deletion
facts.value: Object-class minimum billed capacity, retained days and early-deletion fees are not applicable.

facts.label: vector/index limits
facts.value: Optional external pgvector v0.8.5 supports PostgreSQL 13+; vector values allow up to 16,000 dimensions, while HNSW/IVFFlat vector indexes allow 2,000 and halfvec indexes 4,000.

facts.label: embedding and reranking extras
facts.value: Hosted embedding/reranking model quotas or tariffs are not applicable to core PostgreSQL. Vector generation and optional reranking require separately selected software/model compute or an external provider.

facts.label: run limits and pricing
facts.value: Optional pg_cron v1.6.7 defaults cron.max_running_jobs to 32. Default execution uses local libpq connections; background-worker mode is optional and limited by max_worker_processes. Jobs share database CPU/RAM.

facts.label: run limits and pricing
facts.value: Vendor per-run/invocation/CPU-second tariffs and packaged per-job RAM/vCPU reservations are not applicable to this self-hosted distribution.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Hosted signup, card, trial, account/country eligibility and paid-seat conditions do not apply to this software distribution.

facts.label: primary type and other roles
facts.value: Researcher classification: self-hosted open-source object-relational SQL database server. It also supports JSON/JSONB, extensible types, text search, replication and optional specialized extensions.

facts.label: included backend services
facts.value: Core provides SQL databases, functions/procedures/triggers, database roles, notifications and backup/replication tools. Application-user login, object delivery and general app-worker hosting are separate application responsibilities.

facts.label: app connection options
facts.value: Client/server connections use TCP/IP or local Unix-domain sockets; default TCP port is 5432 and listen_addresses defaults to localhost. A new server process handles each connection.

facts.label: app connection options
facts.value: The base distribution includes libpq (C) and ECPG (embedded C). Other language interfaces are separate projects, potentially with different licenses; psql is the interactive client.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: pg_hba.conf authenticates by connection type, client address, database and role; the first matching rule applies, with no later fallback if authentication fails. No matching rule denies access.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Raw initdb defaults to trust authentication unless configured otherwise; cluster-creation docs recommend a superuser password and scram-sha-256 or another suitable method. OS packages may provide their own setup convention.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Core SSL/TLS support is configurable and ssl defaults off. Administrators must enable certificates/TLS and require secure connection rules; storage-at-rest encryption can be supplied at filesystem/block level or through application/column encryption.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Roles and object/column grants control access. Row-level security must be enabled per table; absent a policy it then defaults to denying rows. Superusers/BYPASSRLS always bypass it; table owners normally bypass unless forced.

facts.label: engine and query model
facts.value: Native PostgreSQL object-relational SQL engine, researched against PostgreSQL 18/18.6 documentation. It supports relational constraints, JSON/JSONB, arrays, functions and extensible types; it is not merely a wire-compatible replacement.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: MVCC transactions provide committed-data isolation. Default Read Committed gives each ordinary SELECT a statement-start snapshot; two SELECTs in one transaction can see different committed data. Read Uncommitted behaves as Read Committed.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: Repeatable Read keeps a transaction snapshot and disallows phantom reads; Serializable adds serialization-anomaly protection. Applications must handle retries after serialization failures. Sequence changes are not rolled back like ordinary table updates.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: Durability depends on WAL/storage settings: fsync protects crash recovery; synchronous_commit defaults on and waits for local WAL flush. With configured synchronous standbys it can also wait for remote durability or application; asynchronous modes can lose recent acknowledged transactions.

facts.label: test environments and branches
facts.value: Separate databases/instances and dumps/restores support test environments. CREATE DATABASE can copy a template database, but the template cannot have other active sessions; database-level settings/grants are not all copied.

facts.label: replicas and failover
facts.value: Streaming/log-shipping standbys and hot-standby read queries are supported; replication can be asynchronous or configured synchronous. Asynchronous replicas can lag and lose unshipped commits after primary loss.

facts.label: replicas and failover
facts.value: Core does not supply the failure-detection software that decides a primary failed and notifies/promotes a standby. Promotion tools exist; correct failover needs external coordination/fencing and reconstruction of the standby topology.

facts.label: live updates and offline sync
facts.value: LISTEN/NOTIFY signals connected listeners after commit; identical channel/payload signals within one transaction can collapse. Default payload must be shorter than 8,000 bytes; this is a signal to fetch data, not a full row transport/offline sync protocol.

facts.label: live updates and offline sync
facts.value: A built-in end-user offline-write queue, conflict-resolution policy and durable reconnect/replay service were not established in the core architecture/notification/replication docs.

facts.label: extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: Core index families include B-tree, Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN; PostgreSQL has full-text search. Extensions add functions/types/index methods; external extension files and their own licenses must be installed/maintained.

facts.label: upload and file limits
facts.value: Managed multipart/resumable object upload limits are not applicable.

facts.label: S3 and other API compatibility
facts.value: A hosted S3 object-operation compatibility matrix is not applicable.

facts.label: delivery and private files
facts.value: Bundled public/private buckets, signed asset URLs, custom domains and CDN prices are not applicable.

facts.label: filters and mixed search
facts.value: Optional pgvector supports SQL filters with exact/ANN distance search; ANN post-filtering can reduce returned neighbors, and iterative scans are configurable. Its hybrid examples combine PostgreSQL full-text retrieval with vector search using rank fusion or a cross-encoder.

facts.label: execution model and languages
facts.value: Core functions/procedures execute within the database; optional external pg_cron v1.6.7 schedules SQL inside PostgreSQL 10+. It requires installation, shared_preload_libraries and a restart, then CREATE EXTENSION.

facts.label: delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: pg_cron can run different jobs in parallel but only one occurrence of a particular job at a time; another scheduled occurrence queues until the prior run completes. It does not run jobs in hot standby, and starts them on promotion.

facts.label: delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: A standard pg_cron automatic retry/backoff, dead-letter and failed-run replay guarantee was not established in its versioned README or the core/project policy pages.

facts.label: schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Optional pg_cron supports cron expressions, intervals of 1–59 seconds, last-day-of-month syntax and configurable timezone (GMT by default). Definitions are stored in cron.job; it may be installed in one database per cluster, with schedule_in_database for other databases.

facts.label: logs and run history
facts.value: pg_cron run details are in cron.job_run_details and are not automatically cleaned; users can delete their own history. Core log collection/rotation/deletion is operator-configured and has no hosted retained-day entitlement.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Run PostgreSQL binaries on a supported OS with a persistent data directory and dedicated OS account. Packages/installers or source builds are available; source needs a C99 compiler and build tools/libraries, while prebuilt package requirements differ.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The operator handles OS/database updates, access/TLS, monitoring, vacuum/analyze, disk/WAL/log growth, backup retention and restore tests. Minor upgrades replace binaries/restart; major upgrades need pg_upgrade, dump/reload or another documented migration method.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: A universal safe production minimum CPU/RAM/disk size was not published in the inspected build, architecture, connection/limits and maintenance docs. Capacity must be chosen for data, indexes, connections, active queries and recovery needs.

facts.label: regions and data location
facts.value: A vendor region catalogue or managed database/backup residency guarantee is not applicable. The operator chooses primary data-directory, server, replica and backup locations.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: pg_dump exports one database as SQL or archive formats; SQL restores through psql, archives through pg_restore. pg_dumpall also preserves cluster-wide roles/tablespaces. Dumps can move across machines/architectures and usually into newer major versions.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: DROP DATABASE removes its catalogue entries and data directory and cannot be undone. It is not executable from the target database or inside a transaction block; existing connections normally block it, with a conditional FORCE option.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Hosted account-erasure deadlines or provider-managed backup-deletion windows are not applicable. Operators must manage their own exports, archives, replicas and logs; the project's privacy policy governs website/community information.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: Core provides SQL dumps, filesystem backups and continuous archiving. pg_dump makes a consistent single-database snapshot without blocking ordinary readers/writers; pg_dumpall includes globals but does not synchronize snapshots across databases.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: PITR requires a base backup plus an unbroken retained WAL archive. Operators configure archiving and retention; it is not enabled as a free managed daily backup schedule. Archive gaps and archive delays constrain recoverability.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: WAL recovery does not restore manually edited postgresql.conf, pg_hba.conf or pg_ident.conf changes. Logical extension dumps use CREATE EXTENSION and require extension control/library files on the destination.

facts.label: file recovery and protection
facts.value: Managed object versioning, bucket locks and file undelete entitlements are not applicable.

facts.label: identity and old names
facts.value: PostgreSQL; Postgres is also an official project name. Earlier names include POSTGRES and Postgres95; the PostgreSQL name was adopted in 1996.

facts.label: hosting and license
facts.value: PostgreSQL License: permissive, BSD/MIT-like. Use, copy, modification and distribution for any purpose are allowed without fee/written agreement, provided the required copyright/license notices are retained.

facts.label: lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: Active community project. Version policy currently lists 18.6 as the current PostgreSQL 18 patch; supported stable major versions are 14–18. The project supports each major for five years.

facts.label: lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: PostgreSQL 14 reaches end of support on 12 November 2026; PostgreSQL 13 already reached EOL on 13 November 2025. These are major-version retirements, not a shutdown of PostgreSQL.

facts.label: lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: PostgreSQL 19 RC1 was announced on 15 October 2026; RC2 is planned for 12 November and GA for 19 November 2026, subject to release-blocking issues. RC builds are for testing, not production.

facts.label: vendor home and main markets
facts.value: A single commercial vendor headquarters/market assignment is not applicable: this record concerns the PostgreSQL Global Development Group community project, with governance by its Core Team and other committees.

facts.label: support and service promises
facts.value: Community support includes documentation, mailing lists and IRC; commercial professional services are provided by separate companies. The software license disclaims warranty and any obligation to provide maintenance/support/updates.

facts.label: support and service promises
facts.value: A project-hosted database SLA, paid-plan support response schedule and database-service status page are not applicable to the software distribution.

facts.label: free offer type
facts.value: A lasting Free tier is advertised: $0/month, no card, no expiry for claimed/Console-created databases, within workspace quotas. Temporary unclaimed databases are a separate expiring access path.

facts.label: free limits
facts.value: Free workspace: 200,000 database operations/month, 2 GB database storage and up to 50 databases. These are workspace allowances, not 2 GB and 200,000 operations multiplied by 50.

facts.label: free limits
facts.value: Optional Compute Free: 1M requests/month, 360 GB-hours provisioned memory, 4 active vCPU-hours and 10 GB outbound bandwidth/month; no usage billing.

facts.label: inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: Unclaimed create-db instances default to deletion after 24 hours; TTL can be set from 30 minutes to 24 hours. Claiming removes that automatic expiry; Console/claimed databases have no fixed time limit advertised.

facts.label: inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: Claimed Free databases scale idle compute to zero and wake on the next query, without a manual wake step. Terms separately allow inactivity reclamation of preview environments but give no fixed period there.

facts.label: least paid commitment
facts.value: Starter: $10/workspace/month base, 1M database operations, 10 GB storage, up to 1,000 databases, 7-day daily backups and spend limits. It is the smallest listed paid plan; no seat fee is advertised.

facts.label: least paid commitment
facts.value: Pro: $49/month, 10M operations/50 GB storage; Business: $129/month, 50M operations/100 GB. Both list 1,000 databases. Pro retains 7 days of snapshots; Business 30 days.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Database excess operations: Starter $8/M, Pro $2/M, Business $1/M. Excess database storage: $2.00, $1.50 and $1.00 per GB/month respectively. Database execution duration and egress do not create separate database compute/transfer charges.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Direct/native usage counts each SQL query, including SELECT 1. Prisma ORM usage is documented as one Prisma Client query even if it expands to several SQL statements; array transactions can count as one, interactive component queries separately.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Optional Compute paid rates: $1/M requests after plan allowance, $0.006/GB-hour memory, $0.064/active-vCPU-hour CPU and $0.025/GB internet outbound. Starter/Pro/Business include 5M/20M/100M requests, but no paid-plan memory/CPU/bandwidth allowance.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Terms bill purchased services monthly by card, excluding taxes; refunds are discretionary credit only. Annual contracts have separate upfront/renewal rules; marketplace billing mechanics follow the reseller's payment terms.

facts.label: idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: Database usage is operations/storage, so zero operations means no operation overage, while retained storage overages and any paid workspace base remain. Optional Compute scales idle instances to zero; kept-awake instances retain memory charges.

facts.label: data transfer costs
facts.value: Prisma Postgres data transfer is unlimited/included on every plan, with no separate database egress charge. Optional Compute internet outbound is separate: Free 10 GB/month, paid $0.025/GB; incoming requests do not count as outbound bandwidth.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: When a Free workspace uses 200k database operations, read/write queries stop until the next calendar-month reset or upgrade. One non-renewing 24-hour grace activation per workspace permits export/use; blocked data is not deleted.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: Paid plans advertise an enforceable spend limit set in Console; free-hosting guidance says queries stop at it. Terms permit pausing/restricting apps, databases or other resources when a spend limit is reached.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: Exact spend-limit accounting delay, treatment of retained-storage/base fees, exclusions and behavior at the Free storage limit were not established in the checked sources.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: Compute Free is never usage-billed; when a workspace passes a free meter limit its apps pause until the next month or an upgrade.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: Pooled concurrent limits: Free 10, Starter 100, Pro 500, Business 1,000. Listed direct limits: 10, 10, 50, 100. Docs additionally reserve five direct connections for platform operations; no unqualified usable-direct calculation is made.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: Pooled queries time out at 10 minutes; direct connections have no provider query-duration timeout documented here. Pooled idle connections close after 60 minutes; session state is not retained across transaction boundaries.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: A managed per-record maximum and maximum paid database size beyond included allowances were not established.

facts.label: storage prices
facts.value: Object Store storage-class/GB-month rates and plan storage allowances are explicitly not published yet.

facts.label: file request and retrieval prices
facts.value: Object Store upload/list/read/retrieval tariffs and any request billing blocks were not published in the inspected material.

facts.label: file request and retrieval prices
facts.value: Image transformations are ordinary Compute routes using Bun.Image and incur normal Compute requests/memory/CPU/outbound usage; no separate managed image-transformation meter is described.

facts.label: minimum storage and early deletion
facts.value: Object minimum billed size/capacity, minimum retention and early-deletion pricing were not established.

facts.label: vector/index limits
facts.value: pgvector is supported/enabled with CREATE EXTENSION vector, but installed extension version, maximum indexed/stored dimensions, vector/index counts and managed namespace limits were not published in the inspected docs.

facts.label: embedding and reranking extras
facts.value: An included embedding/reranking model, token allowance or model-price schedule was not established.

facts.label: run limits and pricing
facts.value: Compute has 60 seconds to send the first response bytes. A started streaming response can continue; after timeout the handler may still run, while its request is no longer in flight and the instance can sleep unless held awake.

facts.label: run limits and pricing
facts.value: Paid Compute separately meters requests, provisioned memory while running/held awake, active CPU and outbound bytes. Waiting can retain memory billing even with negligible active CPU.

facts.label: run limits and pricing
facts.value: Selectable per-instance/per-job memory/CPU shape, maximum concurrency, a universal background-run duration cap and minimum billing increments were not established.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Free claimed databases require no credit card; create-db can provision an unclaimed temporary database with no account/card. Keeping it requires a Prisma account. Paid services use monthly card billing or authorized marketplace billing.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Free-production guidance conflicts: the dedicated free-hosting page permits small production apps, while the database FAQ's sample-cost section describes Free as evaluation-only/not meant for production.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Users must have legal contracting age and must not be barred under relevant laws. Terms prohibit fee/limit circumvention, competitive service construction and specified abusive uses; Free scope/features may change.

facts.label: primary type and other roles
facts.value: Researcher classification: hosted serverless SQL database. Optional same-platform Compute HTTP hosting and Object Store expand the backend; they have separate capabilities/meters and must not be treated as free database entitlements.

facts.label: included backend services
facts.value: Database includes PgBouncer, Studio/data viewing, Query Insights and plan-dependent backups. Optional Compute hosts TypeScript HTTP apps; project Object Store supports files.

facts.label: included backend services
facts.value: A native app-user authentication service and MAU-based allowance were not established in the checked product modules.

facts.label: app connection options
facts.value: Any PostgreSQL client can use native TLS TCP: pooled.db.prisma.io:5432 for application queries; db.prisma.io:5432 for direct/admin/session workloads. Prisma ORM is optional.

facts.label: app connection options
facts.value: The first-party @prisma/ppg serverless driver uses HTTP/WebSockets, with @prisma/adapter-ppg for Prisma ORM or raw SQL. It accepts direct-format credentials but does not open TCP; keep credentials server-side.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: TLS is mandatory for database connections. Every generated credential uses the same database user and has full access; it cannot be made read-only or limited to particular tables/schemas/roles. Custom PostgreSQL roles are not supported.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Generating a credential leaves existing ones valid. After rotation the old password can still work; explicitly delete it to stop new logins. Already-open sessions may survive deletion; contact support for suspected active leaked sessions.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Object Store has per-bucket read/read_write access keys enforced by storage; the secret is returned once. Presigned URLs allow temporary client access without handing out bucket credentials.

facts.label: engine and query model
facts.value: Current GA is managed PostgreSQL 17 using a unikernel-based architecture, with standard PostgreSQL clients and native SQL. Earlier EA PostgreSQL 16 databases are a retired migration path.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: Transactions are supported through native/ORM clients and the serverless driver's transaction/batch APIs, which handle BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK. PgBouncer retains a backend connection for the transaction, then releases it.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: The ORM v7 transaction guide supports isolation-level configuration, inherits the database's configured default, and lists PostgreSQL ReadCommitted as the engine default. Client timeout defaults can be shorter than the hosted direct-query limit.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: Actual managed isolation parameters, synchronous-replication acknowledgement rules and a failover data-loss/RPO guarantee were not established.

facts.label: test environments and branches
facts.value: Compute preview branches own isolated services and newly created databases when declared in Composer; production data is not copied. Composer postgres() migrations run before startup; rawPostgres()/environment-variable databases require separate migration/isolation setup.

facts.label: test environments and branches
facts.value: Branch creation/deploys are not separately billed, but running previews consume shared plan operations/storage and Compute usage. Deleting a linked Git branch tears down previews; production/default branches are protected from that cleanup.

facts.label: replicas and failover
facts.value: Customer-managed read replica configuration, replica region/topology and automatic failover/recovery-time details were not established in the inspected public sources.

facts.label: live updates and offline sync
facts.value: LISTEN/NOTIFY/session-state workloads are directed to direct connections, not transactional PgBouncer. Optional Compute supports streaming/server-sent responses but currently not inbound WebSocket servers.

facts.label: live updates and offline sync
facts.value: A managed offline-client write queue, reconnect replay and conflict-resolution service was not established.

facts.label: extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: Supported-extension list includes vector/pgvector, pg_search, pg_trgm, pgcrypto, postgres_fdw and others; plpgsql is enabled by default. PostGIS and TimescaleDB are explicitly not supported by the migration guide.

facts.label: extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: Extension custom types can require raw SQL/TypedSQL and customized migrations; the extension guide warns that Studio cannot deserialize tables using types such as VECTOR.

facts.label: upload and file limits
facts.value: Object maximum size, multipart/resumable limits, object-count quota and upload restrictions beyond general acceptable use were not established.

facts.label: S3 and other API compatibility
facts.value: Project Object Store is described as S3-compatible; any S3 SDK/client can be used. The guide demonstrates object writing/reading and presigned delivery; bucket-management API also handles keys.

facts.label: S3 and other API compatibility
facts.value: A full supported-operation compatibility matrix, including multipart/versioning/lock semantics, was not established.

facts.label: delivery and private files
facts.value: Buckets can be attached to project branches, with bucket-scoped read/read_write keys and time-boxed presigned URLs. Preview isolation depends on separate branch-associated buckets and scoped credentials.

facts.label: filters and mixed search
facts.value: Official AI docs confirm storing/querying embeddings alongside relational data. Supported pg_search/pg_trgm add text/fuzzy-search components; a managed hybrid rank-fusion/retrieval API was not established.

facts.label: execution model and languages
facts.value: Optional Compute runs TypeScript/Node.js/Next.js applications on Bun as HTTP services; it does not run arbitrary Python/Go/Docker workloads. waitUntil/KeepAwakeGuard can hold instances for bounded background work.

facts.label: delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: waitUntil/KeepAwakeGuard are explicitly best-effort: they prevent sleep but do not make work durable, retry failures or continue through restarts/deploys. Work that must survive needs persisted progress and a later trigger; repeated steps must be safe.

facts.label: schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Compute has no native cron scheduler currently; native cron is planned for early 2027. Use an external scheduler or Composer cron building block, which adds a scheduler service that never scales to zero.

facts.label: schedules and queue retention
facts.value: A built-in durable message-queue retention period, payload maximum, delayed-run guarantee and replay window were not established.

facts.label: logs and run history
facts.value: Compute version logs are available through service logs, with build output in Console. Logs stream in time-bounded segments and can return FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE for some versions. Query Insights is included for database diagnostics.

facts.label: logs and run history
facts.value: Exact hosted app-log/job-result retained days, storage caps and a durable job replay/history guarantee were not established.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Production self-host operating requirements are not applicable to this managed service. The PGlite-based local development guide is version-scoped development tooling, not the hosted service's production self-host deployment path.

facts.label: regions and data location
facts.value: Six database/Compute region codes are listed: us-west-1, us-east-1, eu-west-3, eu-central-1, ap-northeast-1, ap-southeast-1. Compute is single-region per service; place it with its database. create-db can choose nearest region or accept an explicit region.

facts.label: regions and data location
facts.value: Exact database-backup and Object Store region/replica-placement guarantees were not established.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Export/migrate with pg_dump and pg_restore over the direct host, using PostgreSQL 17 tools. Imports must account for unsupported extensions/custom roles; no-owner/no-privileges avoids source role grants, and RLS policies naming absent roles need work.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
