facts.value: The exact commercial support charge, renewal price, regional tax, and payment schedule were not published in the pages checked.

facts.label: Idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: RabbitMQ Server is a long-running broker process, not a managed serverless service that automatically sleeps or scales to zero between requests.

facts.label: Idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: An operator can stop a self-hosted process, but durable queue data and the host/storage remain the operator’s responsibility; this is not an idle-billing feature.

facts.label: Data transfer costs
facts.value: No RabbitMQ software egress, cross-region, or inter-zone tariff applies to the open-source server. Infrastructure transfer charges depend on the host and topology chosen by the operator.

facts.label: Data transfer costs
facts.value: RabbitMQ clustering is designed for LAN nodes with round-trip time well below 1 millisecond; cross-region cluster topology is not presented as a default deployment.

facts.label: Overages and bill controls
facts.value: There are no open-source vendor overage charges, account spend caps, or RabbitMQ-issued budget alerts for self-hosted usage. Operators must manage their infrastructure bill separately.

facts.label: Overages and bill controls
facts.value: Operators can set connection, channel, queue/stream, message-size, TTL, and queue-length limits to protect a node or tenant; these controls stop/reject work rather than cap an external cloud bill.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: The open-source server has no per-task, invocation, or message usage price. Tanzu licensing is per core and subscription term rather than a public per-message meter.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: Default maximum message body/payload size is 16,777,216 bytes (16 MiB); maximum allowed configuration value is 536,870,912 bytes (512 MiB). Messages above configured maximum are rejected.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: For quorum queues in RabbitMQ 4.4, the default consumer acknowledgement timeout is 1,800,000 ms (30 minutes). The operator can set it globally or by queue policy.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: Max connections and total node channels are configurable and default to unlimited; the per-connection AMQP channel default is 2,047. Operating-system and host capacity still constrain practical use.

facts.label: Run limits and pricing
facts.value: RabbitMQ publishes no single throughput figure that applies across queue types, payload sizes, durability, disk, consumers, and cluster size. Streams documentation says throughput falls with larger messages and more replicas.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Open-source binaries and source are publicly available; using the self-hosted server does not require a RabbitMQ account, card, trial, or hosted signup. No form was submitted.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: The software is identified under MPL-2.0, with some OCF files under Apache-2.0. No paid commercial edition is required merely to download the open-source distribution.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Commercial support and Tanzu features require a Broadcom commercial support/license entitlement. The program document limits use to the licensed core count and subscription term.

facts.label: Signup and use restrictions
facts.value: A complete country eligibility list for buying Tanzu RabbitMQ was not found in the RabbitMQ contact page, Broadcom terms/licensing pages, or the product program document checked.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: Our classification: message broker and job queue; messages are routed through exchanges into queues for consumers.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: Secondary roles include publish/subscribe messaging, request/reply, and event streaming through RabbitMQ Streams.

facts.label: Primary type and other roles
facts.value: RabbitMQ provides message storage and delivery, not application database, file storage, user authentication service, or general-purpose job execution. Those components remain the operator's or application’s responsibility.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: The open-source server includes the broker, exchanges, queues, virtual hosts, user/permission management, and optional plugins such as management and Prometheus metrics. It is not a general application backend bundle.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Open-source RabbitMQ supports classic queues, quorum queues, and streams. Quorum queues and streams replicate; classic queues are non-replicated in RabbitMQ 4.x.

facts.label: Included backend services
facts.value: Tanzu adds separate enterprise features. The 4.4 announcement lists automatic quorum leader migration, JMS topics over AMQP 1.0, and exchange federation v2 as commercial-only additions.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: Core protocols include AMQP 0-9-1 and AMQP 1.0; AMQP 1.0 became a core protocol in 4.0.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: RabbitMQ Streams has a dedicated binary protocol and client libraries. MQTT 3.1/3.1.1/5.0 and STOMP are available through plugins; 4.4 made STOMP native to the broker.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: Browser clients can connect over WebSocket with AMQP 1.0, MQTT, or STOMP. HTTP message publishing via the management plugin is intended for diagnostics or low-volume use and does not provide reliable delivery.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: RabbitMQ publishes maintained Java, .NET/C#, Erlang, and AMQP 1.0 client documentation; additional community client libraries are linked from its client developer tools.

facts.label: App connection options
facts.value: Default AMQP client ports are 5672 without TLS and 5671 with TLS. Stream protocol uses 5552 and 5551; additional ports are needed for clustering, management, MQTT, STOMP, or plugins when enabled.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: RabbitMQ users authenticate through internal or configured backends; permissions are scoped to virtual hosts and can restrict configure, write, and read access to named queues and exchanges.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: TLS is supported but must be configured for client and cluster links. The official networking/security guides warn operators to restrict inter-node, management, and monitoring ports to the intended networks.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: The management plugin uses HTTP Basic Authentication and normal RabbitMQ permission checks. Management HTTP and Prometheus ports should be protected and not treated as public client endpoints by default.

facts.label: Data access controls
facts.value: RabbitMQ does not supply an external end-user identity store or application record-level authorization. Applications must enforce end-user permissions before publishing or consuming.

facts.label: Execution model and languages
facts.value: RabbitMQ routes and buffers messages; it does not run user job code. The application or worker process runs on infrastructure the developer supplies.

facts.label: Execution model and languages
facts.value: Workers can be written with RabbitMQ-compatible client libraries. Maintained client docs include Java, .NET/C#, Erlang and AMQP 1.0 clients; community libraries exist for other languages.

facts.label: Execution model and languages
facts.value: CloudAMQP and Amazon MQ are examples of separately managed RabbitMQ hosting. They are not RabbitMQ Server plans and their prices are not included here.

facts.label: Execution model and languages
facts.value: The user supplies the runtime and worker scaling; RabbitMQ coordinates messages and acknowledgements but does not autoscale application workers.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Manual acknowledgements let a consumer acknowledge only after processing. Unacknowledged deliveries are requeued if their channel or connection closes, so an application may see duplicates and should make side effects idempotent.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Publisher confirms let publishers learn that the broker has accepted a publish; quorum queue confirms are issued after replication to a quorum of members.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Quorum queues have a default delivery limit of 20 in RabbitMQ 4.0 and later; after exceeding it, a message is dropped or dead-lettered according to queue configuration.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Dead-letter exchanges can receive rejected, expired, over-length, or over-delivery-limit messages. At-least-once dead-lettering is available for quorum queues with configuration; classic queues do not offer that mode.

facts.label: Delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: RabbitMQ provides at-least-once/redelivery patterns, not exactly-once execution of application side effects. A process can complete an effect and fail before its ack reaches the broker.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Messages can expire using a per-queue or per-message TTL in milliseconds; queue expiration can delete an unused queue. Values are configured by the operator, not included as a fixed retention plan.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Queue length can be capped by ready-message count, body bytes, or both. If the configured cap is reached, default overflow drops or dead-letters the oldest messages; reject-publish modes can reject new messages instead.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: The default queue type is classic unless the virtual host overrides it. Non-durable, non-exclusive classic queues are deprecated and disabled by default from 4.3; classic mirroring was removed in 4.0.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Streams are durable append-only logs with configurable max-age and max-length-bytes; retention removes oldest segments and always leaves at least one non-empty segment.

facts.label: Schedules and queue retention
facts.value: RabbitMQ 4.4 quorum queues can accept delayed messages with a future Unix timestamp in milliseconds. The reviewed release, queue, and limit docs do not specify a maximum future delay.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: RabbitMQ is a broker, not a durable job-run history or application log service. Message backlog/replay depends on queue type, consumer state, TTL, and retention configuration.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: The Management plugin keeps short-term statistics: basic samples at 5-second resolution for 1 minute and 1-minute resolution for 1 hour; detailed samples are retained for 10 seconds. It is not long-term run history.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: Server logs are written to operator-configured local destinations; no standard hosted log-retention period or run-history export allowance applies to the open-source server.

facts.label: Logs and run history
facts.value: Tanzu's commercial Stream Browser can inspect stream contents in the Management UI; the open-source server does not include this listed commercial feature.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: RabbitMQ requires Erlang/OTP. Version 4.4.0 supports Erlang 27.0–29.x; use the compatibility page for the exact broker patch/runtime pairing and keep cluster nodes on a compatible major version.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Supported platforms include common Linux distributions, Windows, macOS and openSUSE; supported Erlang runtime is the underlying requirement. The supported-platforms page says very memory-constrained systems under 100 MB RAM are unsupported.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: RabbitMQ recommends at least 4 CPU cores and 4 GiB RAM per node for production, not colocated with other data services or disk/network I/O-heavy applications. Lower specs may suit lightly loaded QA or development. Storage still depends on the workload.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Durable classic, quorum, and stream data use node storage. Streams are disk intensive and the docs recommend fast disks; operators must allocate and monitor storage for retention settings.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The default client port is 5672; TLS AMQP is 5671. Clusters also need peer discovery/distribution ports; stream clients and replication require 5552/5551 and 6000–6500. Expose only the ports used by the chosen deployment.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Cluster nodes need stable, mutually resolvable hostnames and are designed for a low-latency LAN (round trip well below 1 ms). Erlang distribution and cluster ports must pass between nodes.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Operators handle installation, TLS, credentials, upgrades, monitoring, disk capacity, backups, and recovery. RabbitMQ provides CLI, Prometheus, management, and backup/restore guides but does not operate these tasks for a self-hosted server.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Definition exports are JSON. Message-store backup is a separate operation; restore from disk uses the same node name and copying a changing store from a running node risks an inconsistent backup.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: The open-source server has no hosted dashboard, vendor-managed backups, or plan-based regional placement. The optional Management UI and Prometheus endpoint are self-hosted plugins that operators must protect.

facts.label: Operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Commercial Tanzu-only capabilities include extended support and additional plugins; they require the commercial entitlement and are not implied by the open-source binary license.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: Self-hosted data resides on the operator-selected node disks and network. RabbitMQ does not assign a hosted region or guarantee a country for a self-host deployment.

facts.label: Regions and data location
facts.value: A commercial Tanzu deployment also runs on customer-selected supported infrastructure; its location controls are not the same as a RabbitMQ-managed regional service.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Queue/exchange/user/vhost definitions can be exported as JSON using CLI or the management API, and imported into another cluster.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: Message data lives in per-node directories separated by queue type. A disk restore requires the same RabbitMQ node name; renaming nodes is unsupported when quorum queues or streams are present.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: A consistent offline message backup is operator-managed. The docs discourage copying message stores from a running node because messages are changing and the result can be inconsistent.

facts.label: Leaving and deleting
facts.value: There is no RabbitMQ-hosted account whose stored messages can be deleted by the project. The operator controls the server, files, backups, and final deletion; Broadcom's privacy policy covers company interactions separately.

facts.label: Identity and old names
facts.value: RabbitMQ Server is the official open-source broker name used in the current docs, download page, and GitHub repository.

facts.label: Identity and old names
facts.value: The RabbitMQ project is stewarded by Broadcom through VMware Tanzu; current official support pages describe VMware Tanzu as the owner of RabbitMQ.

facts.label: Identity and old names
facts.value: RabbitMQ is not a renamed cloud service. The commercial VMware Tanzu RabbitMQ edition shares the open-source broker core but is a separate product edition.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: Open-source RabbitMQ Server is self-hosted software. The project provides Linux, Windows, macOS, generic binaries, and a community Docker image; the user supplies and operates the host.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: RabbitMQ server and tier 1 (core) plugins use Mozilla Public License 2.0 (MPL-2.0).

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: Some RabbitMQ server OCF files use Apache Software License 2.0; the main LICENSE file points to separate license files for both licenses.

facts.label: Hosting and license
facts.value: VMware Tanzu RabbitMQ is the commercial edition. The official 4.4 release announcement says it adds closed-source plugins over the open-source core; its separate program document licenses by physical core for a subscription term.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: RabbitMQ is active. GitHub marks v4.4.0 as the latest stable server release; the release page dates it 19 October 2026, while RabbitMQ's lifecycle table lists 20 October 2026.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: RabbitMQ 4.4.0 is supported on Erlang/OTP 27.0 through 29.x. Erlang 28 is fully supported from 4.4.0, Erlang 29 support starts at 4.4.0; Erlang 26 has reached end of life and is unsupported.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: RabbitMQ 4.4 community support ends 31 July 2027; the published commercial support end date is 31 October 2028. Commercial dates are marked indicative by RabbitMQ and Broadcom's support portal is authoritative for contract lifecycle.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: RabbitMQ 4.2 is designated LTS. Its community support ended 31 July 2026; the published commercial support date is 30 June 2030, subject to the Broadcom portal and valid commercial entitlement.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: RabbitMQ 3.13 is also an LTS line but is no longer community-supported; published commercial support runs through 31 December 2029. Broadcom identifies 3.13 and 4.2 as LTS.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: The current Release Information table says 4.3 community support ends 31 January 2027. The older Commercial Features table says 30 November 2026. The newer Release Information date is used here; Broadcom's lifecycle portal is authoritative for paid entitlements.

facts.label: Lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: Broadcom completed its acquisition of VMware on 22 November 2023. Current RabbitMQ footer, security page, and support pages use Broadcom/VMware Tanzu branding; no later RabbitMQ sale, shutdown, or retirement notice was found in the project blog, GitHub releases, Broadcom support pages, or Broadcom newsroom search.

facts.label: Vendor home and main markets
facts.value: Current owner/steward is Broadcom through VMware Tanzu. The project is distributed globally; the product pages checked did not specify a RabbitMQ-only home country or an exhaustive list of customer markets.

facts.label: Vendor home and main markets
facts.value: Broadcom's current privacy policy covers personal data collected through Broadcom sites, customer business interactions, and support; it is not a hosted RabbitMQ message-data policy for a server operated on the user's own infrastructure.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: Community users can seek best-effort help through GitHub, Discord, mailing list, and IRC; the public support page gives no OSS service-level agreement (SLA).

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: The 2024 community policy says direct core-team support is for Tanzu license holders, active contributors, and users reporting certain issues with enough detail to reproduce them. Other users can use community channels but should not expect one-to-one vendor support.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: RabbitMQ's current support page characterizes community help as best-effort; the community support policy announcement adds the above limits on direct core-team help. These statements are compatible when public community discussion is separated from guaranteed engineer support.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: Current commercial Tanzu support is described as 24/7/365 expert support; the highest severity issues receive attention within 30 minutes under the published support description.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: Long-term security patches for OSS RabbitMQ are reserved for customers with a valid commercial support license and Tanzu entitlement; older unsupported community releases do not receive community patches.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: RabbitMQ itself is not a vendor-hosted uptime service and publishes no self-hosted uptime percentage. Service availability depends on the operator's nodes, deployment, and recovery design.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: RabbitMQ's security advisory page lists OSS patches and directs commercial customers to Broadcom Security Advisories as authoritative for commercial binaries and dependencies.

facts.label: Support and service promises
facts.value: The Broadcom KB says support for OSS artifacts bundled in Broadcom products depends on support agreements covering those products; support is limited to components Broadcom produced or the RabbitMQ binary inside some third-party artifacts.

apps.name: Railway
apps.line: Hosted database services for PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis and MongoDB.

free.text: Trial $5/30d; new deploys suspended; Free $1/mo; volumes delete 30d after expiry

cells.regions: US, Europe and Singapore; volumes follow services

sql.math: Assumes 0.5 GB of RAM, 0.05 vCPU, a 1.2 GB volume and 5 GB of egress. Per-second rates give $6.525664. Per-minute rates differ.
An always-on idle example assumes 0.5 GB of RAM, 0.05 vCPU and a 1.2 GB volume. The per-second total is $6.275664.

files.math: 100 GB a month of storage costs $1.50. Direct S3 operations and transfer are free. The Hobby workspace has a $5 minimum.

jobs.math: Active job compute is $0.0579. The $5 applies only if workers stop between jobs. Minimum worker, queue and transfer costs are incomplete.

status.label: Security incident
status.text: 2026-10-21; customer env vars exposed, some decrypted; up to 1.85% of workspaces

facts.label: free offer type
facts.value: Advertised offer: one-time $5 trial credit, expiring after 30 days or consumption, then recurring Free with $1/month and no rollover. Current new-customer deployment access is paid-only while trial deployments are suspended.

facts.label: free limits
facts.value: Free after trial: 1 project, 3 services/project, 1 replica/service, up to 1 vCPU and 0.5 GB RAM/service, 1 GB ephemeral disk, 0.5 GB volume and 1 volume/project; 1 bucket/project with up to 10 GB-month/month against the shared $1 credit; 3-day logs. Cron is trial-only.

facts.label: free limits
facts.value: Advertised Trial: 5 projects, 5 services/project, 2 replicas/service, up to 2 shared vCPU and 1 GB RAM/service, 0.5 GB volume, 3 volumes/project, 3 buckets/project and 50 GB-month bucket usage; 7-day logs. $5/30-day credit and current suspension still apply.

facts.label: free limits
facts.value: Limited Trial bucket eligibility conflicts: Free Trial's table and FAQ say buckets can be deployed; Storage Buckets Billing says buckets are unavailable in Limited Trial.

facts.label: inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: Volume retention after plan expiry/cancellation: Free or Trial 30 days after expiry; Hobby 60 days after cancellation; Pro 90 days after cancellation, following warnings. Trial guide specifically says stateful trial volumes are deleted 30 days after credits expire.

facts.label: inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: Eligible Free buckets become unavailable when the $1 credit is exhausted; files are not deleted for that event. Access returns next cycle or after paid upgrade. Trial bucket access is suspended when the trial ends.

facts.label: least paid commitment
facts.value: Hobby: $5/month minimum per subscription with $5 of usage included. Pro: $20/month with $20 included, unlimited workspace seats. Enterprise: custom price. Hobby is the least public paid path for a solo builder; Pro is positioned for production teams.

facts.label: least paid commitment
facts.value: Subscriptions billed in advance, overage in arrears; earlier partial charges possible. Tax/VAT can be added based on billing location. Enterprise agreement expressly excludes taxes. An explicit ISO currency code was not found in the checked public price/billing/legal pages; preserve '$'.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Public service rates: RAM $0.00000386/GB-second; CPU $0.00000772/vCPU-second; volumes $0.00000006/GB-second. Service egress $0.05/GB; buckets $0.015/GB-month. Service builds are free in the plan docs.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Docs express RAM as $10/GB-month ($0.000231/GB-minute), CPU $20/vCPU-month ($0.000463/vCPU-minute), and volume $0.15/GB-month ($0.000003472222222/GB-minute). These rounded unit expressions do not exactly reproduce the public per-second prices, particularly volume storage.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Additional live environments, HA nodes, pooling services and restored database forks consume resources separately. Volumes bill used bytes plus filesystem metadata, approximately 2–3% of capacity; incremental backup-exclusive bytes also bill. Attached capacity is not the only billed data.

facts.label: idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: Always-running databases consume memory and some CPU even with no queries. Optional Serverless sleeps after no outbound packets for at least 5 minutes, typically 5–10 minutes after traffic; a deployment is required after enabling. Internet/private-network traffic wakes it.

facts.label: idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: Sleep reduces running resource usage, but plan minimums and retained volume/bucket/backup data remain billable. A database or HA cluster is not guaranteed to reach zero compute merely because Serverless is enabled.

facts.label: data transfer costs
facts.value: Service public egress, including public database TCP proxy traffic, is $0.05/GB. Same-project private networking avoids that service egress charge. Uploading from a Railway service to a Railway bucket travels over the public network and incurs service egress.

facts.label: data transfer costs
facts.value: Bucket ingress, S3 operations and bucket egress are unlimited/free. Direct signed-link downloads avoid service egress; proxying file responses through app services incurs service egress. PITR archive uploads also count as service egress; archive downloads from the bucket are free.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: Workspace admins can set a custom email alert separately from a hard Compute Usage limit. Alerts do not stop services; the hard limit takes workloads offline, with notifications at 75%, 90% and 100%. CPU/memory replica limits can also crash an undersized service.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: Hard usage limits suspend bucket reads and uploads, but existing stored bucket data continues to be billed. Bucket access resumes after limit increase/removal or next period. Hobby bucket uploads exceeding its 1 TB combined capacity fail.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: Volume defaults: Free/Trial 0.5 GB; Hobby 5 GB; Pro 50 GB. Paid volumes can grow; Pro and above can self-serve to 1 TB, larger needs Enterprise. Per-project volumes: Free 1, Trial 3, Hobby 10, Pro 20 (increase possible), Enterprise unlimited. Each service mounts one volume; ordinary replicas cannot share it.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: Paid compute maxima across replicas: Hobby 48 vCPU/48 GB; Pro 1,000 vCPU/1 TB; Enterprise 2,400 vCPU/2.4 TB. Hobby replica limit conflicts: plan card says up to 5 at 8 vCPU/8 GB each; comparison table and plan docs say 6.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: PostgreSQL PgBouncer defaults to 1,000 client connections and 20 server connections per pooler replica; scale 1–6 pooler replicas. Total server connections must stay within PostgreSQL max_connections. Plan-independent max query/record sizes and the shipped database max_connections value were not established.

facts.label: storage prices
facts.value: Railway Standard object storage: $0.015/GB-month, defined as 30 days, averaged across all bucket instances in the workspace, including environments. Separate from database volumes. Free/Trial usage draws from shared credits; Hobby/Pro usage draws from included plan usage.

facts.label: file request and retrieval prices
facts.value: All S3 API operations are unlimited and free, with no data retrieval fee. Bucket ingress and egress are free. File processing/transformation done in an app consumes app resources and possibly service egress.

facts.label: minimum storage and early deletion
facts.value: Usage is averaged daily and rounded up to the next whole GB-month, e.g. 5.1 bills as 6. No minimum storage-retention period; Standard only. Partial-month storage is averaged, not charged for a full 30 days regardless of use.

facts.label: minimum storage and early deletion
facts.value: A minimum billable object byte size or separate per-object capacity floor was not found.

facts.label: vector/index limits
facts.value: Optional custom pgvector deployment: upstream HNSW supports vector up to 2,000 dimensions, halfvec 4,000, bit 64,000, sparsevec 1,000 nonzero elements. A vector column can hold up to 16,000 dimensions; column and indexed limits differ.

facts.label: embedding and reranking extras
facts.value: Embeddings are supplied by the app; no included Railway database embedding/reranking model allowance or per-token pricing found. Optional model providers or a model service deployed by the user need their own bill.

facts.label: run limits and pricing
facts.value: Functions are Services, so estimate their CPU/RAM using standard service rates and service egress, not the distinct sandbox VM rates. Function source limit: 1 file, 96 KB; Bun is the only Function runtime. Retries/waiting that keep a process alive consume CPU/RAM resources.

facts.label: run limits and pricing
facts.value: Cron does not automatically terminate a deployment: code must finish and close resources. A universal Function request timeout, job wall-time maximum, or app-level task concurrency limit was not found; plan resource/service ceilings apply.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: New account creation requires no card, but deploying currently requires Hobby or Pro. The pricing FAQ accepts credit cards for subscriptions and usage; Enterprise can pay by invoice.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Terms require age 16 or older; users must have legal capacity or parental/guardian permission. Own internal, personal and/or business use is permitted subject to law and the acceptable-use policy; export controls apply. A complete country eligibility list was not found.

facts.label: primary type and other roles
facts.value: Researcher classification: hosted database deployment platform with shared operating duties; SQL, document and key-value databases. Secondary roles: app hosting, files, functions and scheduled jobs.

facts.label: included backend services
facts.value: Native resources: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis and MongoDB templates; persistent volumes, backups, private networking, S3-compatible buckets, general application services, TypeScript/Bun Functions and cron jobs.

facts.label: included backend services
facts.value: Railway Authentication gates public deployment domains behind a login and was announced for Enterprise only. It is distinct from an included end-user identity database for an app.

facts.label: app connection options
facts.value: Apps use each engine's native connection protocol and client libraries through private connection variables. PostgreSQL DATABASE_URL; MySQL MYSQL_URL; Redis REDIS_URL; MongoDB MONGO_URL. Public TCP access is opt-in and creates separate public connection URLs.

facts.label: app connection options
facts.value: General services support many languages through Railpack or a Dockerfile, including JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Go, Ruby, PHP, Rust, Java and C#. Canvas Functions use TypeScript with Bun.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Databases deploy private by default; public TCP access must be added. Private service communication uses encrypted WireGuard tunnels and environment-isolated internal DNS. Keep database credentials server-side in service variables.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: PostgreSQL supports SQL privileges and row policies. RLS must be enabled; owners and BYPASSRLS/superuser roles normally bypass it. Configuring roles, settings or extensions directly moves database-specific configuration outside Railway's stock-template support scope.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Regenerating database passwords/bucket credentials now redeploys services that reference them through Railway variables; hardcoded credentials must be updated manually.

facts.label: engine and query model
facts.value: Native PostgreSQL and MySQL relational engines, Redis key-value/in-memory engine, and MongoDB document engine are deployed as containers from the documented images. These are engine deployments, not one common SQL compatibility layer.

facts.label: engine and query model
facts.value: PostgreSQL HA supports pinned major versions 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18; latest is not accepted for HA. One-click major upgrades support source majors 14–17 to newer published majors on official images, with downtime and backups. Changing a major tag alone does not migrate data.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: For the PostgreSQL 18 example: native transactions; Read Committed is the default, each statement reads a committed snapshot. Repeatable Read and Serializable are available; Read Uncommitted behaves as Read Committed. Serializable workloads must handle transaction retries.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: Railway's PostgreSQL HA uses streaming replication and automatic leader election. A Railway-specific published promise of synchronous commit, maximum replica lag, or zero lost acknowledged writes during failover was not found.

facts.label: test environments and branches
facts.value: Persistent staging/dev environments and temporary PR environments isolate service configuration. PR environments are deleted on PR merge/close; each live environment incurs real resource usage.

facts.label: test environments and branches
facts.value: Duplicate Environment copies services, variables and configuration; that description does not promise a copy-on-write database-data branch. PITR can create an independent sibling database fork, billed as another service; cutover is manual.

facts.label: replicas and failover
facts.value: Stock templates offer opt-in HA for PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis and MongoDB. Engine guides describe Patroni/etcd/HAProxy for Postgres, Group Replication for MySQL, Sentinel for Redis and a MongoDB replica set. Each adds running components and storage.

facts.label: replicas and failover
facts.value: PostgreSQL HA defaults: primary plus 2 streaming replicas (2–7 configurable), 3 etcd nodes (3/5/7/9), and 3 HAProxy instances (2–5; Trial limited to 2). Automatic promotion reroutes connections; in-flight connections drop. Reverting to standalone retains detached volumes and their storage charges.

facts.label: live updates and offline sync
facts.value: PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY needs a dedicated session/unpooled URL, or session pooling; default PgBouncer transaction mode does not support it. It is a database notification mechanism, not automatic offline mobile synchronization.

facts.label: live updates and offline sync
facts.value: A native durable offline client sync package, offline write queue and conflict-resolution contract were not found for the database offering.

facts.label: extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: Default PostgreSQL templates intentionally do not add popular extensions. The guide links separate pgvector, PostGIS and TimescaleDB marketplace options. Custom images such as PostGIS/TimescaleDB are incompatible with the stock PostgreSQL HA conversion and major-upgrade flow.

facts.label: upload and file limits
facts.value: Multipart uploads and direct browser presigned uploads are documented; a backend can set content-type and content-length conditions on signed POST uploads. Hobby aggregate capacity 1 TB; uploads over the cap fail. Pro aggregate storage is unlimited in pricing.

facts.label: upload and file limits
facts.value: Maximum single-object size, single-PUT ceiling, multipart part-size/count limits and a separate resumable-upload contract were not found.

facts.label: S3 and other API compatibility
facts.value: Documented S3 subset includes Put/Get/Head/Delete, List/List V2, Copy, presigned URLs, tagging and multipart. Unsupported: server-side encryption API, object versioning, object locks and bucket lifecycle configuration. New buckets use virtual-hosted URLs; older buckets may use path-style.

facts.label: delivery and private files
facts.value: Buckets are private; public buckets are not supported. Serve direct signed object URLs, valid up to 90 days, or authorize through an app proxy. Browser clients can use signed direct uploads rather than receive the bucket's permanent credentials.

facts.label: delivery and private files
facts.value: Backend proxy routes can use CDN caching/custom app delivery; service egress applies. A native bucket custom-domain/CDN configuration and corresponding separate delivery tariff were not established.

facts.label: filters and mixed search
facts.value: Upstream pgvector supports exact nearest-neighbor search, HNSW/IVFFlat approximate indexes, SQL WHERE filters and hybrid search with PostgreSQL full-text search. Approximate-index filters run after scanning and may return fewer rows unless tuned.

facts.label: execution model and languages
facts.value: Railway hosts general container workers and cron services in supported languages. Canvas Functions run one TypeScript file using Bun and can handle webhooks, simple APIs and cron jobs; ordinary services can use virtually any Docker-compatible stack.

facts.label: delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: If a cron service is still running at its next scheduled time, Railway skips that run. Services default to On Failure with at most 10 restarts; paid plans can configure any number, while Free/Trial cannot choose Always and have a 10-restart limit.

facts.label: delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: No native queue delivery contract covering ordering, deduplication, exactly-once processing, dead-letter retention or automatic replay was found for cron/Functions. Durable task persistence/retries require app design or a deployed queue service.

facts.label: schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Cron uses five fields in UTC, with every pair of scheduled runs at least 5 minutes apart, including hour boundaries. Execution can vary by minutes; exact schedule timing is not guaranteed. Hobby allows 50 cron jobs/project, Pro 100; lasting Free has no cron feature.

facts.label: schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Queue-message retention, delayed-message horizon and maximum task payload were not published for native cron/Functions in the checked pages.

facts.label: logs and run history
facts.value: Logs: Free 3 days; Trial/Hobby 7 days; Pro 30 days; Enterprise up to 90 days. Dashboard/explorer/CLI access; 500 lines/second/replica limit, excess dropped. Forward logs yourself for longer retention. Functions retain deployed source versions for redeploy/rollback.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Self-hosted Railway platform edition: not applicable to this hosted offering. The user can bring database images, but must manage their major upgrades, disk capacity, schema, queries, indexes, monitoring alerts and opt-in protection. Changes to stock image/config/roles/extensions can move DB operations outside support scope.

facts.label: regions and data location
facts.value: Service regions: California us-west2; Virginia us-east4-eqdc4a; Amsterdam europe-west4-drams3a; Singapore asia-southeast1-eqsg3a. A volume follows its service's region; moving it causes migration downtime.

facts.label: regions and data location
facts.value: Bucket region is selected at creation and cannot then be changed. Each environment has a separate bucket instance and credentials. Exact physical backup/snapshot placement and a full bucket-region matrix were not found.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: PostgreSQL can export through native pg_dump as SQL/custom/directory archives and restore with psql/pg_restore; globals such as roles need pg_dumpall. S3 Get/List download bucket objects separately; Railway CLI also downloads volume files.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Deleted volumes can be restored via emailed link during the 48-hour deletion period; after 48 hours deletion is permanent. Deleted buckets remain restorable through project Activity for 52 hours, then objects are permanently destroyed.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Account can be deleted through account settings. Terms warn account termination may destroy content and recovery is not promised. DPA provides return/deletion of personal data at customer choice on agreement end, with legal/impracticability exceptions. No exact universal account/database/backup purge deadline found.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: Volume backups are opt-in manual or scheduled. Daily every 24 h retained 6 days; weekly every 7 days retained 27 days; monthly every 30 days retained 89 days. Multiple schedules can coexist; incremental exclusive bytes bill at volume rates.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: Backup restore stages a replacement volume in the same project and environment, retaining the unmounted original. Wiping a volume deletes all its backups. Manual backup size is limited to 50% of volume total size unless grown or support changes the limit.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: PostgreSQL PITR: pgBackRest weekly full and daily differential backups plus WAL, last 4 full backups retained, roughly 4-week restore window after first base backup. MySQL: daily logical full backup plus binlogs retained 7 days; latest point trails real time about 1 minute, target granularity 1 second.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: PITR is opt-in; no separate PITR feature fee, but compressed bucket archive storage and service egress uploads bill, plus restore service/volume resources. Restore creates a new single-node sibling, even from HA; original stays untouched. Re-enable PITR and reconvert to HA if needed.

facts.label: file recovery and protection
facts.value: Object versioning, object locks and bucket lifecycle configuration are explicitly unsupported. Whole-bucket deletion has 52-hour restoration, but this does not promise restoration of an individual overwritten/deleted object. Database volume backups do not cover independent bucket contents.

facts.label: identity and old names
facts.value: Railway databases is the database offering within Railway, operated by Railway Corporation. Official platform: https://railway.com/ .

facts.label: hosting and license
facts.value: Hosted Railway services run database containers with attached persistent volumes. Railway owns its platform service; this is not an offered self-host edition of Railway.

facts.label: lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: Operating for existing customers. New signups reopened November 2, 2026 at 19:19 UTC; a paid Hobby or Pro subscription is required before new customers deploy. Free-trial deployments remain temporarily unavailable.

facts.label: lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: 2026-10-21 security incident: Railway confirms unauthorized access to internal systems, an unauthorized query of encrypted environment variables and decryption of a subset of stored secrets. Its preliminary report says at most 1.85% of workspaces (about 100,000) had variables potentially compromised; it could not identify every decrypted variable and was still notifying affected/high-risk customers. Railway says user accounts were not accessed; source-code access remained unconfirmed in the preliminary report.

facts.label: lifecycle and access stage
facts.value: At check time, external network blocks were affecting access from some networks; the status page's latest update was November 4, 22:03 UTC. Railway attributes these blocks to forged-source scanning and says it found no link to the October incident.

facts.label: vendor home and main markets
facts.value: Railway Corporation lists a San Francisco, California, United States contact address.

facts.label: support and service promises
facts.value: Trial/Free/Hobby: community support at Central Station, no guaranteed reply. Pro: Railway help there, usually within 72 hours, without SLO or app debugging. Enterprise/Business Class support has additional commitments; public status is https://status.railway.com/ .

facts.label: support and service promises
facts.value: Pricing lists availability targets of 99.9% Hobby, 99.99% Pro and 99.999% Enterprise. Database docs say no published database uptime SLA today. These targets are not a Hobby/Pro service-credit contract.

facts.label: support and service promises
facts.value: Published Enterprise Agreement Exhibit A sets 99.5% monthly service availability using commercially reasonable efforts, with excluded scheduled/third-party events and credit bands 10%/25%/100% below 99.5%/98.5%/95%. Claim notice within 72 hours of discovering outage.

apps.name: Redis Cloud
apps.line: Hosted Redis database for key-value data, vector search, and message streams.

free.text: 30MB, 100 ops/s, 5GB/mo; evaluation deletes after 14d idle; Free rule unclear

cells.metered: Essentials from USD $5/mo; Pro min USD $200/mo
cells.regions: AWS, GCP and Azure; plan coverage varies
cells.selfhost: Yes, Redis 8+ offers an AGPLv3 option

sql.math: 1 GB of data needs a 2.5 GB plan with replication (nominal size). The exact regional quote and add-ons are not available.
The kept 1 GB workload is more than Free's 30 MB. The paid regional subscription price is not available, and it stays due while idle.

files.math: Redis Cloud does not offer general file storage.

jobs.math: Both the Streams broker and outside workers are needed. Worker hosting, message size, commands and retention are not priced.

facts.label: free offer type
facts.value: Cloud Free is advertised as always $0 with a 30 MB database. Pro separately advertises the first $200 free; that is promotional credit, not a recurring free Pro subscription.

facts.label: free offer type
facts.value: Self-hosted Redis has no hosting allowance: software may be used under the selected release license, while machines, storage, backup, transfer and operations remain the user's costs.

facts.label: free offer type
facts.value: The public Pro $200 promotion's precise expiry, redemption conditions and eligible charges were not established from pricing, billing-credit documentation or the current Cloud Agreement.

facts.label: free limits
facts.value: Cloud Free: one database per account, 30 MB, 30 simultaneous connections, 100 ops/sec and 5 GB total monthly network bandwidth.

facts.label: free limits
facts.value: Free has no replication or data persistence and cannot back up/export through the Cloud console. The price card offers community support and best-effort availability.

facts.label: inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: Evaluation instances may be deleted after 14 days without account activity; expired unconverted evaluations/previews lose access and associated data under §2.8.

facts.label: inactivity, pause, and deletion
facts.value: How the advertised always-free database is classified under evaluation terms, its exact idle pause/deletion interval and a guaranteed retention/resume window remain unresolved.

facts.label: least paid commitment
facts.value: Cloud Essentials starts at USD 5/month, with a displayed approximate USD 0.007/hour headline. This is a global starting offer; its exact size/provider/region combination was not established.

facts.label: least paid commitment
facts.value: Cloud Pro has a minimum USD 200/month. Its USD 0.014/hour starting headline is not the entire subscription price; Annual pricing is a separate negotiated commitment.

facts.label: least paid commitment
facts.value: An exact AWS us-east-1 Essentials/Flex/Pro quote could not be extracted with the available public read-only calculator retrieval.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Essentials pricing scales with plan size; current RAM plans span 250 MB–12 GB and Flex plans 1–100 GB. HA changes usable capacity, so equal nominal plan sizes are not equal unique-data capacity. Flex Essentials fixes the RAM share at 10%; other Flex configurations can adjust the RAM/Flash tradeoff.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Pro charges depend on Redis Billing Units (RBU), memory, provisioned throughput, HA and region; the report shows RBU count × price/hour × active hours and a minimum-subscription adjustment.

facts.label: billing meters
facts.value: Public full-precision regional RBU rates, short-period rounding and the complete treatment of all add-on charges were not established.

facts.label: idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: Committed expenditure remains payable regardless of use. Deleting a database while keeping its subscription can continue charges; the subscription must also be deleted to stop its payment.

facts.label: idle compute and scale to zero
facts.value: An automatic paid compute scale-to-zero mode with durable retained data and a published wake/idle threshold was not found.

facts.label: data transfer costs
facts.value: Essentials RAM monthly total plan bandwidth: Free 5 GB; 250 MB 100 GB; 1 GB 200 GB; 2.5 GB 400 GB; 5 GB 800 GB; 12 GB 2000 GB.

facts.label: data transfer costs
facts.value: Essentials Flex monthly total bandwidth: 1 GB 50 GB; 2.5 GB 100 GB; 5 GB 200 GB; 12 GB 500 GB; 25 GB 1000 GB; 50 GB 2000 GB; 100 GB 4000 GB.

facts.label: data transfer costs
facts.value: Pro network costs are charged at subscription level. The Agreement passes network charges through as specified in the Transaction; account reports can show them with up to 72 hours of delay.

facts.label: data transfer costs
facts.value: Exact internet, cross-zone and cross-region unit rates, and any financial overage tariff for Essentials bandwidth, were not established.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: Essentials warns before limits; the official quota guide describes alerts around 80–85% usage, possible throttling/dropped connections, and rejected clients at the connection ceiling. Upgrading does not reset current-cycle usage.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: Cloud memory policy can evict keys; its documented default is volatile-lru. Choosing no eviction rejects additional values at the memory limit instead of deleting keys.

facts.label: overages and bill controls
facts.value: Metrics alerts monitor capacity, connections, throughput and latency. A guaranteed account-wide financial cap, including network/support/add-ons, was not found.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: Paid RAM Essentials current size/connection/throughput pairs: 250 MB / 256 / 1000 ops/sec; 1 GB / 1024 / 2000; 2.5 GB / 2500 / 4000; 5 GB / 5000 / 8000; 12 GB / 10000 / 16000.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: Cloud Pro's comparison lists up to 50 TB and no fixed database-level connection limit. Actual connections remain constrained by infrastructure, database configuration and workload, and may be limited for stability.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: Self-hosted Redis 8.10.3 example configuration documents default maxclients 10000, affected by file-descriptor resources. Its configurable bulk-string protocol limit is normally 512 mb.

facts.label: capacity and connection limits
facts.value: An exact managed per-key/value ceiling and uniform Search-index or namespace limit across every Cloud plan/version were not established.

facts.label: storage prices
facts.value: Redis database memory/Flash capacity is not a separately sold file/object-storage class; no applicable bucket GB-month tariff is recorded.

facts.label: file request and retrieval prices
facts.value: Object upload/list/retrieval request classes and image-processing tariffs do not describe the Redis command database interface.

facts.label: minimum storage and early deletion
facts.value: Object minimum-retention and archive early-deletion pricing do not apply to this database offer; subscription minimums are covered in C12–C14.

facts.label: vector/index limits
facts.value: Native vector indexes support FLAT, HNSW and, from Redis 8.2, SVS-VAMANA. Vector fields live in HASH or JSON data; algorithm/type availability depends on release.

facts.label: vector/index limits
facts.value: Documented vector types include FLOAT32/FLOAT64, FLOAT16/BFLOAT16 (Search 2.10+) and INT8/UINT8 (Redis 8.0+). DIM must be positive and exactly match query-vector dimensions.

facts.label: vector/index limits
facts.value: A universal numeric maximum dimension, vector count or per-tenant/index quota was not established from the inspected vector/schema/Cloud-limit material.

facts.label: vector/index limits
facts.value: Paid Redis Software's Flash Search preview supports HNSW FLOAT32/FLOAT16 with explicit required tuning, but not FLAT/SVS-VAMANA or every in-memory field option; at least 20% RAM is recommended.

facts.label: embedding and reranking extras
facts.value: RedisVL can use external embedding APIs or local models; optional rerankers likewise use external APIs or local inference. API model requests or local compute are additional dependencies rather than assumed included database capacity.

facts.label: run limits and pricing
facts.value: Cloud broker capacity uses its database plan/RBU, memory, operations, connections and network. No included 0.5-vCPU/0.5-GB worker machine or per-job execution-second tariff is supplied by this queue mechanism.

facts.label: run limits and pricing
facts.value: Lua executes atomically and blocks other server work while running. Self-hosted 8.10.3 documents a default 5000 ms busy-reply threshold; this is not a guarantee that scripts are automatically killed at five seconds.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Public Cloud onboarding supports email activation or Google/GitHub signup. The Free database creation guide offers a 30 MB database; this research created no account.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Direct paid Essentials and Pro creation require a payment method and business address; the documented flow adds a credit card when none is present. Marketplace purchases have separate payment arrangements.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: A universal guarantee that completing Free creation never requires a card, a complete eligible-country list and explicit Free commercial-production permission were not established.

facts.label: signup and use restrictions
facts.value: Evaluation services and previews are for non-production use and normally last 30 days unless a Transaction states otherwise. Privacy excludes under-16 users from the site/products.

facts.label: primary type and other roles
facts.value: Primary directory type: key-value database and cache. Secondary roles: document data, vector/text search, pub/sub and Streams message coordination. These are our labels for the documented capabilities.

facts.label: included backend services
facts.value: Cloud includes the Redis database, managed deployment, database credentials/ACLs, metrics, and plan-dependent persistence, backups and replication. Pro adds dedicated infrastructure, private connectivity and Active-Active options.

facts.label: included backend services
facts.value: Bundled end-user signup/MAU billing, general app file buckets and general-purpose hosted worker machines were not found in this Redis database offer.

facts.label: app connection options
facts.value: Redis uses the binary-safe RESP protocol over TCP (default local port 6379); Unix sockets are possible locally. Redis 7+ core commands support RESP2 and RESP3, with response-type differences.

facts.label: app connection options
facts.value: Documented client languages include Python, JavaScript, Java, Go, C#/.NET, C and Ruby. PHP Predis and Rust redis-rs have best-effort support; community libraries are identified separately.

facts.label: app connection options
facts.value: Cloud's REST API manages resources; the subscription comparison lists it for paid plans and not Free. Application data normally uses Redis clients and the database endpoint.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Database credentials differ from console account users. RBAC can restrict commands, key patterns and Pub/Sub channels through Redis ACLs and assigned roles.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Paid Cloud supports TLS, but the TLS guide says it is not enabled by default; optional mutual TLS uses client certificates.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Free transport-security claims conflict: subscription comparison lists encryption in transit, but the dedicated TLS guide explicitly excludes Free.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Paid Essentials/Pro can use CIDR allow lists; dedicated guidance explicitly excludes Free. The size table nevertheless lists one Free CIDR rule.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Pro private connectivity includes AWS VPC peering/Transit Gateway/PrivateLink and GCP VPC peering/Private Service Connect, subject to regional configuration.

facts.label: data access controls
facts.value: Self-hosted Redis should be restricted to trusted clients/networks. Protected mode and binding/firewalls protect an unconfigured instance; ACLs and TLS must be configured for the deployment.

facts.label: engine and query model
facts.value: Self-hosted Redis is an in-memory data-structure server with Redis commands rather than SQL tables. Redis 8 integrates search, JSON, time series and probabilistic components under the Redis 8 license choice.

facts.label: engine and query model
facts.value: Cloud database versions are managed separately from the open-source release stream; patch updates are automatic. Essentials minor updates are automatic; supported Pro versions allow the documented minor-upgrade choice, while major versions are customer controlled until end-of-life enforcement.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: MULTI/EXEC executes queued commands sequentially without another client's interleaving; WATCH provides optimistic checks. Runtime errors after EXEC do not roll back successful commands in the transaction.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: Self-hosted replication is asynchronous by default. WAIT can wait for replica acknowledgments but does not make the system strongly consistent; acknowledged writes can still be lost during failover.

facts.label: transactions and consistency
facts.value: Self-hosted Redis Cluster partitions keys into slots; multi-key operations generally require keys in the same slot, and hash tags can colocate related keys. Cluster uses asynchronous replication with documented write-loss windows.

facts.label: test environments and branches
facts.value: Separate Cloud subscriptions/databases and a local Redis installation can provide isolated test environments. New/upgraded Essentials subscriptions have one database; additional environments need their own eligible subscription or local instance.

facts.label: test environments and branches
facts.value: Native copy-on-write database branching, branch quotas and automatic preview-branch deletion were not found in this offer's inspected docs.

facts.label: replicas and failover
facts.value: Free Cloud has no replica. Paid Essentials and Pro offer none, single-zone or multi-zone replication with automatic failover when replication is enabled.

facts.label: replicas and failover
facts.value: Essentials nominal plan size includes the replica: a 1 GB plan with replication allocates 512 MB to data and 512 MB to its copy. Pro instead asks for dataset size and calculates the replication memory limit.

facts.label: replicas and failover
facts.value: Cloud Pro advertises multi-region Active-Active and annual-plan deployment options. These are paid managed features, separate from self-hosted Redis Open Source Sentinel/Cluster.

facts.label: replicas and failover
facts.value: Self-hosted Sentinel monitors a non-clustered deployment and promotes replicas on primary failure; Redis Cluster combines partitioning with failover. Both require operator-managed nodes, topology and failure handling.

facts.label: live updates and offline sync
facts.value: Pub/Sub is live, at-most-once delivery: a disconnected subscriber loses messages. Streams retain entries and consumer-group pending state for later delivery/recovery.

facts.label: live updates and offline sync
facts.value: An integrated browser/mobile offline database with local reads/writes, automatic reconnection merge and app-user conflict resolution was not found in the inspected Redis offer.

facts.label: extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: Redis Search indexes HASH or JSON fields using text, tags, numbers, geography and vectors. Search schema/command support depends on database version and edition.

facts.label: extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: Cloud calculator FAQ says hosted Flex currently lacks Search/vector search and Active-Active. Separately, Redis Software Search on Flex is a limited preview requiring cluster 8.2.6+ and database 8.8+.

facts.label: extensions and specialized indexes
facts.value: The deprecated-components documentation lists RedisGraph, RedisGears and JavaScript Triggers and Functions as deprecated. New projects should verify migrations instead of relying on old module tutorials.

facts.label: upload and file limits
facts.value: Redis strings can hold binary data, but they use the Redis command/protocol and memory limits. This is not a documented multipart/resumable upload endpoint; the self-hosted bulk-string default is configurable.

facts.label: S3 and other API compatibility
facts.value: Cloud can write RDB backups to S3/GCS/Azure Blob and FTP(S) destinations. Redis's application data endpoint remains RESP; an S3 backup destination does not make it an S3-compatible object API.

facts.label: delivery and private files
facts.value: Public/private object delivery, signed file URLs and CDN buckets are outside the documented Redis database offering.

facts.label: filters and mixed search
facts.value: Search supports nearest-neighbor/range retrieval combined with text, numeric, geographic and tag metadata filters. Field/key filtering and database ACLs are separate controls for tenant access.

facts.label: filters and mixed search
facts.value: FT.HYBRID, introduced in Redis Open Source 8.4, combines text and vector results using reciprocal-rank fusion or weighted linear fusion. Check target Cloud engine/command support; Software Flex preview explicitly excludes this command.

facts.label: execution model and languages
facts.value: Streams coordinate consumers that run in the application or external workers; Redis is the message/data server. Native server-side EVAL and Redis Functions execute sandboxed Lua 5.1, not general hosted JavaScript/Python worker machines.

facts.label: delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Consumer groups track delivered/unacknowledged entries; XACK acknowledges, and pending/claim operations let consumers recover work. A worker can execute a task again after failure, so applications still need safe duplicate handling.

facts.label: delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Redis 8.6 adds idempotent message production/deduplication support. That producer-side capability is version-specific and does not eliminate application retries or prove exactly-once end-to-end job execution.

facts.label: delivery and failure behavior
facts.value: Pub/Sub has at-most-once delivery and no durable disconnected-subscriber recovery. It should not inherit consumer-group acknowledgment/replay behavior from Streams.

facts.label: schedules and queue retention
facts.value: Streams retention is configured by trimming length or minimum entry ID; entries and pending state consume database capacity and inherit persistence/eviction behavior. Acknowledging a message normally does not itself delete it.

facts.label: schedules and queue retention
facts.value: A native general-job cron scheduler, delayed-job timezone contract, fixed queue-retention day allowance and separate universal message-payload ceiling were not established.

facts.label: logs and run history
facts.value: Cloud database metrics cover operations, latency, memory, keys, connections and network, with graphs out to three months at coarser resolution and configurable threshold alerts.

facts.label: logs and run history
facts.value: An included per-job execution log/result history, automatic dead-letter dashboard and fixed failed-job replay-history retention were not found.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Redis Open Source can run through Docker or platform packages on Linux/macOS; the current Windows guide uses Docker. Persistent data needs durable storage, and the operator handles configuration, upgrades, security, backups and recovery.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Self-hosted operators choose RAM, disk and CPU for keys, allocator/index overhead, persistence rewrites and replicas. A universal safe minimum for the directory's workloads was not established and no cheapest-server price is invented.

facts.label: operating requirements and feature gaps
facts.value: Paid Redis Software has separate proprietary terms and features such as Flex/managed enterprise controls. Redis Open Source does not include Redis Cloud's hosting, managed backup/control plane, support contract or uptime credits.

facts.label: regions and data location
facts.value: Cloud offers selectable AWS/GCP regions with plan-specific coverage; examples available to Essentials and Pro include AWS us-east-1, eu-west-1 and ap-south-1, plus GCP us-central1 and asia-south1.

facts.label: regions and data location
facts.value: Azure Redis Cloud Essentials lists east-us and west-us; Pro on Azure is offered through the separate Azure Managed Redis product. AWS me-central-1 is temporarily unavailable despite its matrix entry.

facts.label: regions and data location
facts.value: Multi-zone Cloud replication needs a region with at least three zones. Zone settings are fixed at subscription creation; changing them requires a new subscription and migration. Backup location is separately configured.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Paid Cloud exports RDB snapshots to configured external storage; sharded databases produce an RDB per shard. Importing supported RDB data overwrites the target dataset.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Cloud deletion requires Account Owner and is documented as unrecoverable. Deleting the last database and deleting its subscription are separate choices.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: A numeric deadline for removal from all Redis active systems, backups and retained logs was not published in the inspected deletion/contract/privacy material.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Self-hosted RDB/AOF files and compatible Redis clients provide a migration path; the operator controls source files, off-box backups and secure disposal.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Account deletion is separate from database deletion and subscription cancellation. The Owner must remove resources, other users, API keys and payment methods, clear invoices, and then submit the privacy request; legal retention exceptions remain.

facts.label: leaving and deleting
facts.value: Direct subscriptions are canceled in Redis Cloud after database deletion; AWS/GCP marketplace mappings and Heroku/Vercel integrations require their channel-specific steps. Accrued charges remain payable.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: Cloud persistence: Free has none; paid Essentials offers AOF every second or snapshots at 1/6/12-hour intervals; Pro also allows AOF every write. Turning persistence off exposes data to loss when a database goes down.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: Paid Essentials supports manual exports and 24-hour scheduled backups; Pro supports manual exports and schedules every 24/12/6/4/2/1 hours. Default concurrent backups are limited to four per subscription.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: Cloud backups use RDB files, one per shard, in configured S3/GCS/Azure Blob/FTP(S) storage. Redis-managed repositories are limited to Heroku/Vercel-created databases; customer destinations need suitable permissions.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: A universal included backup-retention day count, complete backup-storage tariff and arbitrary point-in-time recovery guarantee were not established.

facts.label: backups and restore
facts.value: Self-hosted persistence supports RDB snapshots and AOF logs; when both are enabled, AOF is used for restart recovery. Off-box copies, retention, restore tests and persistent disk setup are the operator's responsibility.

facts.label: file recovery and protection
facts.value: Object version history, bucket object locks and file undelete are outside this database scope; RDB/AOF database recovery is recorded in D05.

facts.label: identity and old names

facts.label: hosting and license
facts.value: AGPLv3 is the OSI-approved copyleft option. RSALv2 restricts commercializing the software or providing its functionality as a managed service; SSPLv1 adds service-source obligations when offering it as a service.

facts.label: hosting and license
